item.title: Claude Cowork and Claude Code With Local Models: 2026 Setup Guide
item.category: "Local AI" , "AI Coding Tools" , "Self-Hosted AI" , "Developer Tools" , "Privacy" , "Open Source Models" , "Automation" , "AI Hardware"
item.description: Ollama connects Claude Desktop and Claude Code to local models through an Anthropic-compatible API. Here is the correct setup for each, the environment variable most guides omit, which models to use in September 2026, and which features stay cloud-only.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>Claude’s agentic tools now run against models on your own hardware, with no API key, no subscription, and no data leaving the machine.</strong> Ollama exposes an Anthropic-compatible API, and both Claude Code and Claude Desktop connect to it in a few commands.</p> <p><em>Most guides get one important detail wrong. They describe Claude Cowork, then hand you setup steps which configure the command-line tool instead. Those are two different integrations, and only one of them gives you Cowork.</em></p> <p>This guide covers both paths separately, the environment variable the popular tutorials skip, which models to pair with each in September 2026, and the features which stay cloud-only no matter what you configure.</p> <h2 id="the-short-answer"> <a href="#the-short-answer" title="The Short Answer">The Short Answer</a> <a href="#the-short-answer" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Short Answer">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Ollama connects to Claude in two distinct ways, and picking the wrong one is the most common reason people finish a setup guide with a working terminal and no Cowork.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Integration</th> <th>What You Get</th> <th>Setup Path</th> <th>Platform</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Claude Desktop</strong></td> <td>Cowork, subagents, web search, auto mode</td> <td>Ollama app, then <strong>Apps</strong> and <strong>Connect Claude</strong></td> <td><strong>macOS only</strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Claude Code</strong></td> <td>The CLI coding agent with tool calling and file edits</td> <td><code>ollama launch claude</code>, or environment variables</td> <td>macOS, Linux, Windows</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>If you want Cowork, use the Claude Desktop integration.</strong> It is a graphical flow in the Ollama app, and it is macOS-only while Windows support is still listed as coming soon.</p> <p><strong>If you want an agent in your terminal, use Claude Code.</strong> One command does it.</p> <p><em>Both are free. The only cost is the hardware and the electricity.</em></p> <h2 id="two-integrations-not-one"> <a href="#two-integrations-not-one" title="Two Integrations, Not One">Two Integrations, Not One</a> <a href="#two-integrations-not-one" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Two Integrations, Not One">#</a> </h2> <p>The confusion starts with the naming. <strong>Claude Cowork is a feature inside Claude Desktop</strong>, not a separate application, and not a synonym for Claude Code.</p> <p>Ollama’s documentation lists them on separate pages under separate headings. Claude Desktop sits under <strong>Assistants</strong>, alongside OpenClaw and Hermes. Claude Code sits under <strong>Coding</strong>, alongside OpenCode, Cline, and Codex CLI.</p> <p>The distinction matters because the setup differs completely:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Claude Desktop</strong> is configured through the Ollama application interface. You do not touch a shell profile.</li> <li><strong>Claude Code</strong> is configured through environment variables or a single launch command.</li> </ul> <p>A guide which tells you to export <code>ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL</code> and run <code>claude</code> has configured the command-line tool. If you followed those steps expecting the Cowork desktop experience, <strong>nothing in your setup is broken. You configured a different product.</strong></p> <h2 id="setup-claude-desktop-and-cowork"> <a href="#setup-claude-desktop-and-cowork" title="Setup: Claude Desktop and Cowork">Setup: Claude Desktop and Cowork</a> <a href="#setup-claude-desktop-and-cowork" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Setup: Claude Desktop and Cowork">#</a> </h2> <p>This path runs through the Ollama application rather than the terminal.</p> <h3 id="prerequisites"> <a href="#prerequisites" title="Prerequisites">Prerequisites</a> <a href="#prerequisites" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Prerequisites">#</a> </h3> <ul> <li><strong>Ollama installed</strong>, on macOS. Windows support is documented as coming soon.</li> <li><strong>A model downloaded first</strong> if you plan to run locally. For a cloud model, sign in to Ollama and enable cloud models. Some cloud models require a paid plan.</li> <li><strong>Claude installed.</strong> If it is missing, Ollama offers to download it during setup.</li> </ul> <h3 id="the-steps"> <a href="#the-steps" title="The Steps">The Steps</a> <a href="#the-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Steps">#</a> </h3> <ol> <li>Open Ollama and select <strong>Apps</strong>.</li> <li>Select <strong>Connect Claude</strong>.</li> <li>Follow the setup prompts. Install Claude if prompted, and restart it when asked.</li> </ol> <p>This is the whole flow. To change models afterward, open <strong>Ollama Settings</strong>, go to <strong>Apps</strong>, choose your models, and select <strong>Restart Claude</strong>.</p> <h3 id="what-carries-over"> <a href="#what-carries-over" title="What Carries Over">What Carries Over</a> <a href="#what-carries-over" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Carries Over">#</a> </h3> <p>Ollama’s documentation lists four features as supported through this integration:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Cowork</strong>, for completing difficult tasks</li> <li><strong>Subagents</strong>, for splitting larger tasks across agents</li> <li><strong>Web search</strong>, provided by default through Ollama’s search</li> <li><strong>Auto mode</strong>, which lets the agent decide when to ask before making changes</li> </ul> <p><em>Cowork appears in this list, which is the part worth noting. It is available through this integration and not through the command-line one.</em></p> <h3 id="disconnecting"> <a href="#disconnecting" title="Disconnecting">Disconnecting</a> <a href="#disconnecting" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Disconnecting">#</a> </h3> <p>Disconnecting restores Claude’s previous configuration, so the change is not destructive.</p> <ul> <li>Through the interface, open <strong>Apps</strong> and disconnect Claude, then restart Claude when prompted.</li> <li>From a terminal, run <code>ollama launch claude-desktop --restore</code>.</li> <li><strong>Quitting Ollama while Claude is connected also restores Claude’s usual configuration.</strong> If you want the local setup to persist, leave Ollama running.</li> </ul> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/claude-desktop-ollama-integration-flow.webp", "caption": "Diagram showing the Ollama application Apps panel connecting to Claude Desktop, with model selection routed through Ollama settings and a restore path back to the original configuration", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-09-23 04:19:53.614206649 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b499.171906960", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-09-23 04:19:53.614206649 +0000 UTC m=+499.171906960"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/claude-desktop-ollama-integration-flow.webp" alt="Diagram showing the Ollama application Apps panel connecting to Claude Desktop, with model selection routed through Ollama settings and a restore path back to the original configuration"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h2 id="setup-claude-code-from-the-cli"> <a href="#setup-claude-code-from-the-cli" title="Setup: Claude Code From the CLI">Setup: Claude Code From the CLI</a> <a href="#setup-claude-code-from-the-cli" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Setup: Claude Code From the CLI">#</a> </h2> <p>This is the path covered by almost every guide, and for terminal work it is the right one.</p> <h3 id="the-one-command-method"> <a href="#the-one-command-method" title="The One-Command Method">The One-Command Method</a> <a href="#the-one-command-method" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The One-Command Method">#</a> </h3> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>ollama launch claude </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The command sets the required environment variables, points Claude Code at your local Ollama instance, and starts it. Choose a model from the list and press Enter. To name the model up front, add the flag:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>ollama launch claude --model qwen3.5 </span></span></code></pre></div><p><em>The wrapper handles the environment for you. Read the next section anyway, because knowing what it sets is how you debug it later.</em></p> <h3 id="the-manual-environment-variables"> <a href="#the-manual-environment-variables" title="The Manual Environment Variables">The Manual Environment Variables</a> <a href="#the-manual-environment-variables" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Manual Environment Variables">#</a> </h3> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN<span style="color:#f92672">=</span>ollama </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY<span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">""</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL<span style="color:#f92672">=</span>http://localhost:11434 </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>claude --model qwen3.5 </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>The second line is the one popular guides omit.</strong> Setting <code>ANTHROPIC_API_KEY</code> to an empty string prevents an existing real key in your environment from interfering with the local connection. If you publish a guide with the variables printed on a page and leave the line out, readers with a key already exported get a confusing failure.</p> <p>To avoid modifying your shell profile, pass everything inline:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN<span style="color:#f92672">=</span>ollama ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL<span style="color:#f92672">=</span>http://localhost:11434 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY<span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">""</span> claude --model kimi-k2.7-code:cloud </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Two details worth knowing from the official documentation:</p> <ul> <li><strong><code>ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN</code> carries the bearer authentication</strong>, which is why it holds the literal string <code>ollama</code> in local mode.</li> <li><strong>Claude’s own settings files override shell variables.</strong> If a connection behaves oddly after you export new values, check those settings and then run <code>/status</code> inside Claude Code to see which endpoint is in use.</li> </ul> <h3 id="connecting-straight-to-ollama-cloud"> <a href="#connecting-straight-to-ollama-cloud" title="Connecting Straight to Ollama Cloud">Connecting Straight to Ollama Cloud</a> <a href="#connecting-straight-to-ollama-cloud" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Connecting Straight to Ollama Cloud">#</a> </h3> <p>You do not need Ollama installed at all for this route. Set an API key and point Claude Code at Ollama’s hosted endpoint:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL<span style="color:#f92672">=</span>https://ollama.com <span style="color:#ae81ff">\ </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN<span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">"</span>$OLLAMA_API_KEY<span style="color:#e6db74">"</span> <span style="color:#ae81ff">\ </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>ANTHROPIC_API_KEY<span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">""</span> <span style="color:#ae81ff">\ </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>claude --model glm-5.3-flash </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>One caveat applies here.</strong> Ollama’s documentation notes hosted web search and advanced tool controls are not fully supported on this route. Basic chat, file edits, and tool calling work with compatible models.</p> <h2 id="model-choices-for-september-2026"> <a href="#model-choices-for-september-2026" title="Model Choices for September 2026">Model Choices for September 2026</a> <a href="#model-choices-for-september-2026" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Model Choices for September 2026">#</a> </h2> <p>The model lineup moved a long way during 2026, so advice written in the spring is worth rechecking. Here is where things stand now.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Model</th> <th>Type</th> <th>Context</th> <th>Why Pick It</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Qwen3.8 27B</strong></td> <td>Local, 18 GB</td> <td>256K</td> <td>Current best local all-rounder with vision, tool calling, and thinking control</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Qwen3 Coder Next</strong></td> <td>Local, MoE 80B total / 3B active</td> <td>256K</td> <td>Built for always-on coding agents, non-thinking mode for speed</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Qwen3.6 35B A3B</strong></td> <td>Local, MoE 35B / 3B active</td> <td>262K</td> <td>Apache 2.0 and efficient on modest memory</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>kimi-k2.7-code:cloud</strong></td> <td>Cloud</td> <td>Large</td> <td>Coding-focused cloud model with no local hardware requirement</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>glm-5.3-flash</strong></td> <td>Cloud</td> <td>Large</td> <td>The model Ollama’s own documentation reaches for first</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Start with Qwen3.8 27B if you have the memory.</strong> It runs locally with a 256K context window, native vision, tool calling, and thinking you toggle per request. On a card with 24 GB or more it is a comfortable daily driver.</p> <p><strong>Start with a cloud model if you do not.</strong> Pointing Claude Code at a hosted model costs nothing to try and removes the hardware question entirely, at the price of your code leaving the machine.</p> <h3 id="a-warning-about-ternary-models"> <a href="#a-warning-about-ternary-models" title="A Warning About Ternary Models">A Warning About Ternary Models</a> <a href="#a-warning-about-ternary-models" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Warning About Ternary Models">#</a> </h3> <p>If you read our <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="local AI 2026 guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/local-ai-2026-build-your-rig-now/"> <a href="/articles/local-ai-2026-build-your-rig-now/" rel="follow me" >local AI 2026 guide</a> </span> </strong>, you know ternary Bonsai 2 27B runs a full 27B model in <strong>5.53 GiB</strong>. It is tempting to reach for it here.</p> <p><strong>It will not work with this workflow.</strong> The ternary kernels live in Prism ML’s llama.cpp fork, and stock Ollama cannot load those files. A command like <code>ollama launch claude --model Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B</code> fails before inference starts. Use the standard Qwen3.8 27B pack for Claude Code, and reserve the ternary packs for a runtime built to handle them.</p> <p><em>Convenience and maximum efficiency pull in different directions here. The integrated tooling wants a standard GGUF.</em></p> <h2 id="set-a-64k-context-before-blaming-the-model"> <a href="#set-a-64k-context-before-blaming-the-model" title="Set a 64K Context Before Blaming the Model">Set a 64K Context Before Blaming the Model</a> <a href="#set-a-64k-context-before-blaming-the-model" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Set a 64K Context Before Blaming the Model">#</a> </h2> <p>Ollama’s documentation gives one direct instruction for repository work: choose a model and <strong>set a 64k or larger context window</strong>, raising it further for larger repositories.</p> <p>The reason is mechanical. Claude Code pulls file contents, diffs, and command output into the context window. A model left at a small default runs out of room partway through a task, and the failure looks like a reasoning problem rather than a settings problem.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Context</th> <th>What It Handles</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Under 32K</td> <td>Single-file edits and quick questions</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>64K</strong></td> <td>Multi-file work in a modest repository</td> </tr> <tr> <td>128K</td> <td>Larger repositories and long command output</td> </tr> <tr> <td>256K</td> <td>The full window on Qwen3.8 27B</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>If Claude Code loses the thread halfway through a task, check the context setting before you swap models.</em></p> <h2 id="verify-tool-calling-in-one-command"> <a href="#verify-tool-calling-in-one-command" title="Verify Tool Calling in One Command">Verify Tool Calling in One Command</a> <a href="#verify-tool-calling-in-one-command" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Verify Tool Calling in One Command">#</a> </h2> <p>Tool calling is the difference between an agent and a text generator, and it is worth confirming rather than assuming.</p> <p>Once Claude Code is running, ask it:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Read the current directory and list all files </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>If it lists real files, tool calling works.</strong> If it replies it would read the directory and describes what it expects to find, tool calling is not wired up. You are talking to a chat model with a coding prompt attached, and no amount of prompting fixes it.</p> <p>Work through the fixes in this order:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Switch to a model with confirmed tool support.</strong> Not every model implements it, and the difference is not visible from the parameter count.</li> <li><strong>Confirm the environment points at Ollama.</strong> Run <code>ollama --version</code> and check <code>ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL</code> is set to your local endpoint.</li> <li><strong>Run <code>/status</code> inside Claude Code.</strong> Any base URL or credential in Claude’s own settings overrides the shell variables you recently exported.</li> </ol> <h2 id="what-stays-cloud-only"> <a href="#what-stays-cloud-only" title="What Stays Cloud-Only">What Stays Cloud-Only</a> <a href="#what-stays-cloud-only" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Stays Cloud-Only">#</a> </h2> <p>Know the boundary before rebuilding a workflow around local inference.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Feature</th> <th>With Local Models</th> <th>Cloud</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Chat and file edits</td> <td>Yes</td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Tool calling</td> <td>Model-dependent</td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Subagents</td> <td>Yes</td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Web search</td> <td>Provided through Ollama</td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cowork</strong></td> <td>Through the Claude Desktop integration</td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Auto mode</td> <td>Through the Claude Desktop integration</td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Scheduled prompts</td> <td>Through <code>/loop</code> in Claude Code</td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Three caveats on the local side:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Multi-file reasoning degrades before speed does.</strong> A local model handles one file well, three files acceptably, and a whole repository poorly. Plan the task size around it.</li> <li><strong>Some cloud models require a paid Ollama plan</strong>, and cloud models need you signed in with them enabled.</li> <li><strong>The cloud-direct route has feature limits.</strong> Hosted web search and advanced tool controls are not fully supported when you skip the local installation.</li> </ul> <p><em>Local inference is excellent at bounded, verifiable work and worse at sprawling, ambiguous work. This is a useful line to organize around.</em></p> <h2 id="automate-it"> <a href="#automate-it" title="Automate It">Automate It</a> <a href="#automate-it" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Automate It">#</a> </h2> <p>Two features make this more than an interactive toy.</p> <h3 id="headless-runs-for-scripts-and-ci"> <a href="#headless-runs-for-scripts-and-ci" title="Headless Runs for Scripts and CI">Headless Runs for Scripts and CI</a> <a href="#headless-runs-for-scripts-and-ci" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Headless Runs for Scripts and CI">#</a> </h3> <p>The <code>--yes</code> flag skips the interactive selectors and pulls the model when needed. It requires <code>--model</code>, and anything after <code>--</code> goes straight to Claude Code:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>ollama launch claude --model gemma4:cloud --yes -- -p <span style="color:#e6db74">"how does this repository work?"</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Watch the permission model here.</strong> Claude Code prompts before most actions, so a headless run either needs configured permission rules or an isolated environment. Do not point an unsupervised agent at a repository you care about.</p> <h3 id="scheduled-prompts-with-loop"> <a href="#scheduled-prompts-with-loop" title="Scheduled Prompts With /loop">Scheduled Prompts With <code>/loop</code></a> <a href="#scheduled-prompts-with-loop" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Scheduled Prompts With /loop">#</a> </h3> <p>Inside a Claude Code session, <code>/loop</code> runs a prompt or slash command on an interval:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>/loop 30m Check my open PRs and summarize their status </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>/loop 1h Research the latest AI news and summarize key developments </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>/loop 15m Check for new GitHub issues and triage by priority </span></span></code></pre></div><p><em>This runs while the session is open. It is not a background daemon, so it ends when the session does.</em></p> <h2 id="troubleshooting"> <a href="#troubleshooting" title="Troubleshooting">Troubleshooting</a> <a href="#troubleshooting" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Troubleshooting">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Symptom</th> <th>Likely Cause</th> <th>Fix</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Connection refused</strong></td> <td>Ollama is not running</td> <td>Run <code>ollama serve</code>, and confirm with <code>curl http://localhost:11434/api/tags</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Describes actions instead of performing them</strong></td> <td>The selected model lacks tool calling</td> <td>Switch to a model with confirmed tool support</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>A real API key gets used instead of the local endpoint</strong></td> <td><code>ANTHROPIC_API_KEY</code> is still exported</td> <td>Set it to an empty string, as shown above</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cowork is missing after setup</strong></td> <td>The Claude Code CLI was configured instead of Claude Desktop</td> <td>Use the Ollama <strong>Apps</strong> flow for Cowork</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Generation is slow</strong></td> <td>Context set too high, or a dense model where a sparse one fits</td> <td>Lower the context, then try a mixture-of-experts model</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Exported variables have no effect</strong></td> <td>Claude’s settings files override shell variables</td> <td>Check the settings files, then run <code>/status</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Background requests fail</strong></td> <td>Claude Code reaches for a small model for internal tasks</td> <td>Point the small-model override at the same local model</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>Two of these seven come down to the same thing. Most setup problems are a wrong endpoint or a model without tool calling.</em></p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Claude Desktop and Claude Code are separate integrations.</strong> Cowork lives in Claude Desktop and is configured through the Ollama <strong>Apps</strong> panel on macOS. The CLI path does not give you Cowork.</li> <li><strong>One command starts the CLI route</strong>: <code>ollama launch claude</code>. The manual equivalent needs three variables, and <strong><code>ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=""</code> is the one most guides leave out</strong>.</li> <li><strong>You do not need a local install at all.</strong> Point Claude Code at <code>https://ollama.com</code> with an API key.</li> <li><strong>Set a 64K or larger context before judging a model.</strong> A small window mimics a reasoning failure.</li> <li><strong>Verify tool calling with one request.</strong> If the model describes what it would do, you have a text generator rather than an agent.</li> <li><strong>Ternary Bonsai packs do not work here.</strong> They need Prism ML’s llama.cpp fork, and stock Ollama cannot load them.</li> <li><strong>Disconnecting is safe.</strong> Quitting Ollama restores Claude’s previous configuration, and <code>ollama launch claude-desktop --restore</code> does it from the terminal.</li> </ul> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" item.title: Local AI in 2026: A 27B Model Beats Sonnet 4.6, and the Hardware Window Is Closing
item.category: "Local AI" , "Self-Hosted AI" , "Open Source Models" , "AI Hardware" , "Machine Learning" , "Quantization" , "Homelab" , "Privacy" , "AI Economics" , "Consumer Hardware"
item.description: Qwen3.8 27B and its ternary repack Bonsai 2 27B now outscore Claude Sonnet 4.6 on the aggregate intelligence index while running on one consumer GPU. What changed, what the benchmarks show, and why memory pricing makes waiting the most expensive option.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>A downloadable model which fits on a single consumer graphics card now outscores a frontier API model on the aggregate intelligence index.</strong> Qwen3.8 27B is an open-weight vision-language model released in August 2026. Its ternary repack, Bonsai 2 27B, squeezes the same weights into 5.53 GiB. Together they mark the moment local inference stopped being a hobbyist compromise and became a genuine substitute for a paid API.</p> <p><em>The hardware side of this story is closing fast. Memory prices are the worst they have been in two decades, and they are dragging graphics card prices up with them.</em></p> <p>This article covers what the benchmarks show, what the two models are under the hood, where the open model still loses, and why the next twelve months are the wrong time to wait.</p> <h2 id="the-short-answer"> <a href="#the-short-answer" title="The Short Answer">The Short Answer</a> <a href="#the-short-answer" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Short Answer">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The intelligence gap between a local 27B model and a paid frontier-adjacent API model has closed, and the remaining advantages of the paid model are narrower than the price difference suggests.</strong></p> <p>Three things changed at once:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Open 27B models reached frontier-adjacent scores.</strong> Qwen3.8 27B posts a 33.7 Intelligence Index against Sonnet 4.6 at 30.1, on the same evaluation suite.</li> <li><strong>Ternary quantization cut the memory requirement by roughly two thirds.</strong> Bonsai 2 27B runs the full 27B model in <strong>5.53 GiB</strong>, which fits on cards costing a few hundred dollars.</li> <li><strong>Memory supply went in the wrong direction.</strong> Conventional DRAM contract prices rose <strong>90 to 95 percent</strong> quarter over quarter in early 2026, the steepest quarterly jump TrendForce has recorded, which pushed next-generation GPUs out to 2028.</li> </ul> <p><em>Buying or building now is the cheap option. This is not a sales pitch, it is what the supply data says.</em></p> <h2 id="watch-the-single-gpu-test"> <a href="#watch-the-single-gpu-test" title="Watch the Single-GPU Test">Watch the Single-GPU Test</a> <a href="#watch-the-single-gpu-test" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Watch the Single-GPU Test">#</a> </h2> <p>The claim above deserves a demonstration rather than a table. Bijan Bowen tested Bonsai 2 27B on a single-GPU machine and asked whether it is the best model available for a single card today.</p> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { if (typeof yieldToMain === 'function') { yieldToMain(loadLiteYouTubeScript, "user-visible"); } else { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); } }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style><div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/VideoObject http://schema.org/LearningResource" style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Bonsai 2 27B First Test – Is THIS the BEST Single-GPU AI Model?"> <meta itemprop="description" content="A first look at running the 27B Bonsai 2 ternary model on a single consumer GPU, covering speed, quality, and whether it beats the alternatives."> <meta itemprop="thumbnailUrl" content="https://img.youtube.com/vi/OA5cICIzD-c/maxresdefault.jpg"> <meta itemprop="contentUrl" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OA5cICIzD-c"> <meta itemprop="learningResourceType" content="Concept Overview"> <meta itemprop="educationalLevel" content="High school (US)"> <lite-youtube videoid="OA5cICIzD-c" videotitle="Bonsai 2 27B First Test – Is THIS the BEST Single-GPU AI Model?" videoplay="" nocookie posterloading="lazy" loading="lazy" params=""> <noscript> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OA5cICIzD-c" class="lite-youtube-fallback" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="Bonsai 2 27B First Test – Is THIS the BEST Single-GPU AI Model?"> <span class="lyt-visually-hidden"></span> </a> </noscript> </lite-youtube> </div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": ["VideoObject", "LearningResource"], "name": "Bonsai 2 27B First Test – Is THIS the BEST Single-GPU AI Model?", "description": "A first look at running the 27B Bonsai 2 ternary model on a single consumer GPU, covering speed, quality, and whether it beats the alternatives.", "thumbnailUrl": ["https:\/\/img.youtube.com\/vi\/OA5cICIzD-c\/maxresdefault.jpg"], "contentUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OA5cICIzD-c", "learningResourceType": "Concept Overview", "educationalLevel": "High school (US)" } </script> <p><em>Watch for the output quality rather than the tokens-per-second figure. Speed is the easy part to fix.</em></p> <h2 id="two-names-one-model"> <a href="#two-names-one-model" title="Two Names, One Model">Two Names, One Model</a> <a href="#two-names-one-model" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Two Names, One Model">#</a> </h2> <p>The two models worth understanding here are not competitors. <strong>They are the same weights at two different precisions.</strong></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th></th> <th>Qwen3.8 27B</th> <th>Ternary Bonsai 2 27B</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>What it is</strong></td> <td>The original open-weight model from Qwen</td> <td>A ternary repack of Qwen3.8-27B by Prism ML</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Weights on disk</strong></td> <td><strong>18 GB</strong></td> <td><strong>5.53 GiB</strong> (PTQ1_0) or <strong>6.70 GiB</strong> (PQ2_0)</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Parameters</strong></td> <td>27B dense</td> <td>26.90B, same architecture</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Context</strong></td> <td>256K</td> <td>262,144 tokens</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Vision</strong></td> <td>Yes, native</td> <td>Yes, separate CLIP projector pack</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Tool calling</strong></td> <td>Yes</td> <td>Yes</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>License</strong></td> <td>Apache 2.0</td> <td>Apache 2.0</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Runtime</strong></td> <td>Ollama, llama.cpp, MLX</td> <td><strong>Prism ML’s llama.cpp fork only</strong></td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The Ollama library page for <code>qwen3.8</code> lists the 27B model at <strong>18 GB</strong> with a 256K context window, vision support, tool calling, and a separate MLX build for Apple Silicon. The ternary repack on Ollama is a mirror of Prism ML’s Apache-2.0 GGUF packs, republished with matching checksums.</p> <p><strong>So the practical question is not which model to choose.</strong> It is how much memory you are willing to spend for the same intelligence. The ternary version costs roughly a third of the memory and gives up little.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/local-ai-architecture-comparison.webp", "caption": "Diagram comparing the memory footprint of the same 27B model at 18 GB standard precision against 5.53 GiB in ternary weights, showing both fitting into a single consumer GPU", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-09-23 04:19:53.623935767 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b499.181636078", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-09-23 04:19:53.623935767 +0000 UTC m=+499.181636078"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/local-ai-architecture-comparison.webp" alt="Diagram comparing the memory footprint of the same 27B model at 18 GB standard precision against 5.53 GiB in ternary weights, showing both fitting into a single consumer GPU"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h2 id="the-benchmark-comparison"> <a href="#the-benchmark-comparison" title="The Benchmark Comparison">The Benchmark Comparison</a> <a href="#the-benchmark-comparison" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Benchmark Comparison">#</a> </h2> <p>Artificial Analysis scores both models on the same suite. The results deserve to be read row by row rather than summarized, because the two models win in different places.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Benchmark</th> <th>Qwen3.8 27B</th> <th>Claude Sonnet 4.6</th> <th>Leader</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Intelligence Index</strong></td> <td><strong>33.7</strong></td> <td>30.1</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Coding Index</strong></td> <td><strong>68.1</strong></td> <td>63.0</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Agentic Index</strong></td> <td><strong>45.8</strong></td> <td>31.8</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>GPQA Diamond</strong></td> <td><strong>90.5%</strong></td> <td>87.5%</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Humanity’s Last Exam</strong></td> <td><strong>33.9%</strong></td> <td>33.6%</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>AA-LCR (long context)</strong></td> <td><strong>82.0%</strong></td> <td>80.0%</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>GDPval-AA</strong></td> <td><strong>45.4%</strong></td> <td>36.0%</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>CritPt (research physics)</strong></td> <td><strong>5.4%</strong></td> <td>3.1%</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Non-hallucination rate</strong></td> <td><strong>69.7%</strong></td> <td>51.6%</td> <td>Open</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SciCode</strong></td> <td>46.6%</td> <td><strong>50.1%</strong></td> <td>Sonnet</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>AA-Omniscience accuracy</strong></td> <td>15.6%</td> <td><strong>40.9%</strong></td> <td>Sonnet</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>The open model leads nine of eleven comparable rows, including every aggregate index.</em></p> <h3 id="where-the-open-model-leads"> <a href="#where-the-open-model-leads" title="Where the Open Model Leads">Where the Open Model Leads</a> <a href="#where-the-open-model-leads" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Where the Open Model Leads">#</a> </h3> <p>The three aggregate indexes carry the headline. <strong>Intelligence 33.7 against 30.1, Coding 68.1 against 63.0, Agentic 45.8 against 31.8.</strong> The agentic gap is the widest of the three, and it matters most for anyone running automated multi-step workflows rather than single prompts.</p> <p>For percentile context, Artificial Analysis places Qwen3.8 27B <strong>better than 86 percent of models</strong> on the agentic index and 76 percent on coding. Sonnet 4.6 sits at 68 percent and 72 percent respectively. On graduate-level science reasoning the open model posts <strong>90.5 percent</strong> on GPQA Diamond.</p> <h3 id="where-sonnet-46-still-leads"> <a href="#where-sonnet-46-still-leads" title="Where Sonnet 4.6 Still Leads">Where Sonnet 4.6 Still Leads</a> <a href="#where-sonnet-46-still-leads" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Where Sonnet 4.6 Still Leads">#</a> </h3> <p>Two rows go the other way, and neither is minor.</p> <p><strong>AA-Omniscience measures whether a model answers knowledge questions correctly in the first place. Sonnet 4.6 scores 40.9 percent against 15.6 percent.</strong> This is a wide gap in factual reliability, and it is the strongest single argument for paying for a premium model.</p> <p>The non-hallucination row needs care. Qwen’s 69.7 percent against Sonnet’s 51.6 percent looks like a clean win, and in isolation it is. But the metric describes the share of <em>non-correct</em> answers which avoid fabrication. A model with lower accuracy produces more non-correct answers, so the two percentages describe different populations and are not directly comparable. <strong>Read the accuracy row first.</strong></p> <p>Sonnet also takes SciCode at 50.1 percent against 46.6 percent, and it reports figures on two evaluations the open model’s card does not list, IFBench and Terminal-Bench Hard. Those cannot be compared at all.</p> <h3 id="two-honest-caveats"> <a href="#two-honest-caveats" title="Two Honest Caveats">Two Honest Caveats</a> <a href="#two-honest-caveats" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Two Honest Caveats">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>The release dates are six months apart.</strong> Sonnet 4.6 shipped in February 2026. Qwen3.8 27B shipped in August 2026. A February frontier model against an August open model is not a like-for-like contest.</p> <p><strong>Sonnet 4.6 is no longer Anthropic’s frontier.</strong> Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 now sit above it in the lineup. The open 27B caught a mid-2026 flagship. It has not caught the current top of the stack, and anyone claiming otherwise is overreading the table.</p> <p><em>Benchmarks measure benchmark performance. The only score which matters is the one your own workload produces.</em></p> <h2 id="what-ternary-weights-change"> <a href="#what-ternary-weights-change" title="What Ternary Weights Change">What Ternary Weights Change</a> <a href="#what-ternary-weights-change" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Ternary Weights Change">#</a> </h2> <p>Bonsai 2 is not a smaller model. It is the same 26.90B model at a much lower numerical precision, and the published GGUF metadata makes the trade explicit.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Property</th> <th>Value</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Architecture</strong></td> <td><code>qwen35</code>, hybrid attention with full attention every fourth layer, plus state-space layers</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Parameters</strong></td> <td>26.90B</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Blocks</strong></td> <td>64</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Embedding width</strong></td> <td>5120</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Attention</strong></td> <td>24 query heads, 4 KV heads, key/value length 256</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Context</strong></td> <td>262,144 tokens, RoPE base 1e7</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Weight format</strong></td> <td>Ternary, group size 128. PQ2_0 at 2.13 bits per weight, PTQ1_0 at 1.75</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Vision tower</strong></td> <td>CLIP, 460.73M parameters, shipped as a separate projector pack</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>License</strong></td> <td>Apache 2.0</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Ternary weights mean each parameter carries one of three values instead of sixteen.</strong> The compression is the entire point, and it is why a full 27B model fits in 5.53 GiB rather than 18 GB.</p> <h3 id="measured-throughput"> <a href="#measured-throughput" title="Measured Throughput">Measured Throughput</a> <a href="#measured-throughput" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Measured Throughput">#</a> </h3> <p>Benchmarked with <code>llama-bench</code> on an RTX 5090 32 GB, every layer offloaded, flash attention enabled, mean of three runs:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Pack</th> <th>Weights</th> <th>Prefill (pp512)</th> <th>Decode (tg128)</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>PQ2_0</strong></td> <td>6.70 GiB</td> <td><strong>3802.74 tok/s</strong></td> <td><strong>135.41 tok/s</strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>PTQ1_0</strong></td> <td>5.53 GiB</td> <td>1876.31 tok/s</td> <td>131.41 tok/s</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>PQ2_0 prefills <strong>2.03 times faster</strong> than PTQ1_0 while decode is a statistical tie, so PQ2_0 is the sensible default and PTQ1_0 is for when the last 1.2 GiB matters. Through <code>llama-server</code> with a 65K context, decode held at <strong>136.5 tok/s</strong> on a single streaming request.</p> <p><strong>Decode speed is the figure you feel in daily use.</strong> 135 tokens per second comfortably outruns reading speed. Latency is not the reason to run local inference, since a hosted API is fast enough. Cost, privacy, and control are.</p> <h3 id="the-catch-nobody-mentions"> <a href="#the-catch-nobody-mentions" title="The Catch Nobody Mentions">The Catch Nobody Mentions</a> <a href="#the-catch-nobody-mentions" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Catch Nobody Mentions">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Stock Ollama cannot load these files.</strong> The ternary kernels live in Prism ML’s llama.cpp fork. Verified against Ollama 0.34.2, the load fails with <code>unsupported tensor "output.weight" size overflows</code>. The runtime recognizes the <code>qwen35</code> architecture but has no <code>pq2_0</code> or <code>ptq1_0</code> anywhere in its libraries, and no Hadamard activation runtime.</p> <p>There is a second trap worth knowing before you spend an evening on it. <strong>The F16 pack of this family looks like a safe fallback and is not.</strong> Its tensors are ordinary F16 and F32, so it parses and loads without complaint, then decodes incoherent text. The weights sit in a rotated basis declared in <code>prism.hadamard.*</code> metadata, and a runtime either applies the matching rotation or produces nonsense. At 50.1 GiB the F16 pack also will not fully offload to a 32 GB card.</p> <p><em>Read the model card before downloading. A community mirror is not a supported build, and this one says so plainly on the page.</em></p> <h2 id="the-moe-wave-behind-this"> <a href="#the-moe-wave-behind-this" title="The MoE Wave Behind This">The MoE Wave Behind This</a> <a href="#the-moe-wave-behind-this" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The MoE Wave Behind This">#</a> </h2> <p>Dense 27B models are half the story. Mixture-of-experts models activate a small slice of their parameters per token, which changes the economics again.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Model</th> <th>Total / Active</th> <th>Context</th> <th>Note</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B</strong></td> <td>2.4T / 95B</td> <td>1.0M</td> <td>Open-weight sibling of Qwen3.8 Max</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Qwen3.6 35B A3B</strong></td> <td>35B / 3B</td> <td>262K</td> <td>Apache 2.0, hybrid sparse MoE</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Qwen3 Coder Next</strong></td> <td>80B / 3B</td> <td>256K</td> <td>Open weight, built for always-on coding agents</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Qwen3 Coder Next is the one to watch for local work.</strong> 80B total parameters with only 3B active per token, positioned for always-on agent deployment inside CLI and IDE environments. A model activating 3B parameters generates at the speed of a 3B model while drawing on 80B of stored capability. The upstream notes describe performance comparable to models with 10 to 20 times the active compute.</p> <p><em>The dense 27B is the safe choice today. Sparse models are where the efficiency curve is still bending.</em></p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/local-ai-moe-dense-tradeoff.webp", "caption": "Chart illustrating the difference between a dense 27B model activating all parameters per token and a sparse mixture-of-experts model activating only 3 billion of 80 billion parameters", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-09-23 04:19:53.624474626 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b499.182174927", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-09-23 04:19:53.624474626 +0000 UTC m=+499.182174927"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/local-ai-moe-dense-tradeoff.webp" alt="Chart illustrating the difference between a dense 27B model activating all parameters per token and a sparse mixture-of-experts model activating only 3 billion of 80 billion parameters"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h2 id="the-hardware-window-is-closing"> <a href="#the-hardware-window-is-closing" title="The Hardware Window Is Closing">The Hardware Window Is Closing</a> <a href="#the-hardware-window-is-closing" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Hardware Window Is Closing">#</a> </h2> <p>Here is the part of this story with a deadline attached.</p> <p>Local inference got cheap at the exact moment the memory it depends on started getting expensive. Those two trends are on a collision course, and the collision is already visible in retail pricing.</p> <h3 id="what-happened-to-memory-prices"> <a href="#what-happened-to-memory-prices" title="What Happened to Memory Prices">What Happened to Memory Prices</a> <a href="#what-happened-to-memory-prices" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Happened to Memory Prices">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Conventional DRAM contract prices rose 90 to 95 percent quarter over quarter in the first quarter of 2026</strong>, the steepest quarterly increase TrendForce has on record. NAND flash climbed 55 to 60 percent in the same window.</p> <p>The pressure did not ease. TrendForce data puts second-quarter DRAM up another <strong>58 to 63 percent</strong> and NAND up 70 to 75 percent. Even the third-quarter moderation, DRAM up 13 to 18 percent and NAND up 10 to 15 percent, is inflation stacking on top of two record-setting quarters rather than relief.</p> <p>The cause is structural rather than cyclical. AI data center buildouts absorb memory capacity which used to serve phones, laptops, and game consoles, and memory makers allocate to the higher-margin orders first. Analysts tracking module supply project DRAM chip supply to module makers falling by more than 70 percent in 2027.</p> <p><strong>Intel’s chief executive put a number on it.</strong> Speaking at the AI Infrastructure Summit in Santa Clara on September 15, 2026, Lip-Bu Tan said memory prices had already risen “five, six, and seven times” over prior levels, and warned 70 to 80 percent of a low-cost laptop’s bill of materials now goes to memory alone. He has separately said there is no relief until 2028.</p> <p><em>Independent reporting on the per-area comparison between DRAM wafers and leading-edge logic wafers carries an important caveat. Spot prices are not contract prices, and DDR5 spot procurement is thin enough for the comparison to be suggestive rather than settled. The direction of travel is not in question.</em></p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/local-ai-memory-price-trend-2026.webp", "caption": "Chart showing quarter over quarter DRAM contract price increases through 2026, beginning with a 90 to 95 percent jump in the first quarter and moderating to 13 to 18 percent by the third quarter", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-09-23 04:19:53.624874795 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b499.182575107", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-09-23 04:19:53.624874795 +0000 UTC m=+499.182575107"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/local-ai-memory-price-trend-2026.webp" alt="Chart showing quarter over quarter DRAM contract price increases through 2026, beginning with a 90 to 95 percent jump in the first quarter and moderating to 13 to 18 percent by the third quarter"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h3 id="what-it-did-to-graphics-cards"> <a href="#what-it-did-to-graphics-cards" title="What It Did to Graphics Cards">What It Did to Graphics Cards</a> <a href="#what-it-did-to-graphics-cards" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What It Did to Graphics Cards">#</a> </h3> <p>Memory is a large share of a graphics card’s bill of materials, so DRAM pricing feeds straight into GPU pricing.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Card</th> <th>Early 2025</th> <th>September 2026</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Nvidia RTX 5090</strong></td> <td>$1,999</td> <td><strong>over $5,000</strong></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Asus RTX 5080</strong></td> <td>$1,199</td> <td>$1,595</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>AMD RX 9070 XT</strong></td> <td>roughly $830</td> <td><strong>over $1,037</strong></td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Those increases arrived in coordinated waves through 2026 rather than as isolated spikes. Nvidia raised prices in January, again in May on the RTX 5090 specifically, and again later in the year. AMD followed in August with an increase of at least 10 percent across select Radeon cards and GDDR6 memory kits, attributed directly to memory costs.</p> <p><strong>The next generation slipped instead of shipping.</strong> Nvidia’s RTX 60 series is now expected in 2028, skipping 2027 entirely, with memory availability cited as the cause.</p> <p><em>The card you buy today is not competing against a cheaper card next year. It is competing against a more expensive version of itself.</em></p> <h2 id="why-waiting-is-the-expensive-choice"> <a href="#why-waiting-is-the-expensive-choice" title="Why Waiting Is the Expensive Choice">Why Waiting Is the Expensive Choice</a> <a href="#why-waiting-is-the-expensive-choice" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why Waiting Is the Expensive Choice">#</a> </h2> <p>The usual hardware advice is to wait for the next generation. In a supply-constrained memory market this advice works against you.</p> <p>Three points make the case.</p> <p><strong>Prices are already up and still climbing.</strong> A 90 to 95 percent quarterly jump in DRAM contract prices is not a blip which reverses on a quarterly cycle. TrendForce is forecasting further growth in the third quarter, not decline, and Intel’s chief executive has put relief at 2028.</p> <p><strong>There is no 2027 product to wait for.</strong> When next-generation consumer GPUs slip to 2028, the waiting strategy stretches to a two-year horizon. This is most of a hardware refresh cycle spent waiting for nothing.</p> <p><strong>The models are good enough already.</strong> This is the part which changed in 2026. Two years ago, local hardware bought a visibly compromised experience. Today the same money buys a 27B model at 135 tokens per second with a 262K context window, outscoring a premium API model on the aggregate intelligence index.</p> <p><em>If you were waiting for local models to get good, the wait is over. If you are waiting for hardware to get cheaper, the supply data says you are waiting until 2028.</em></p> <h2 id="what-to-build"> <a href="#what-to-build" title="What to Build">What to Build</a> <a href="#what-to-build" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What to Build">#</a> </h2> <p>Matching hardware to the models above is straightforward, because ternary weights shrank the requirement.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Tier</th> <th>Memory</th> <th>What It Runs Comfortably</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Entry</strong></td> <td>8 to 12 GB VRAM</td> <td>Ternary 27B at 5.53 to 6.70 GiB, with headroom for context</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Practical</strong></td> <td>16 to 24 GB VRAM</td> <td>Full 18 GB Qwen3.8 27B, or the ternary pack at a long context</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Comfortable</strong></td> <td>32 GB VRAM</td> <td>Ternary 27B at the full 262K context, or an 80B MoE at 3B active</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Unified memory</strong></td> <td>64 to 128 GB</td> <td>Larger sparse MoE models on Apple Silicon or a unified-memory desktop</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>A few practical notes which matter more than the tier table:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Buy memory, not the flagship GPU.</strong> The 5.53 GiB ternary pack means the entry tier is genuinely usable. Spending the difference on system RAM and storage helps more than chasing a halo card at 2026 prices.</li> <li><strong>Unified-memory systems are the value play.</strong> A machine with 64 GB or more of shared memory runs larger sparse models at a fraction of the cost of a discrete card with the same capacity.</li> <li><strong>Power and cooling count.</strong> A rig running inference for hours behaves differently from one running benchmarks for minutes.</li> <li><strong>Run the ternary pack alongside a smaller model.</strong> A 3B model answers quick questions while the 27B handles the hard ones.</li> </ul> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <center> <meta itemprop="name" content="simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://ollama.com/tobestyledintro/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B"> <a href="https://ollama.com/tobestyledintro/Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B" title="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" class="markdown-btn" rel="noopener external" alt="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" > <button class="markdown-button"> Download Ternary Bonsai 2 27B </button> </a> <p></p> </center> </span> <h2 id="where-premium-models-still-earn-their-price"> <a href="#where-premium-models-still-earn-their-price" title="Where Premium Models Still Earn Their Price">Where Premium Models Still Earn Their Price</a> <a href="#where-premium-models-still-earn-their-price" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Where Premium Models Still Earn Their Price">#</a> </h2> <p>The case for the premium tier is real, and it is narrower than the marketing suggests.</p> <p><strong>Factual reliability is the honest answer.</strong> AA-Omniscience accuracy is 40.9 percent for Sonnet 4.6 against 15.6 percent for the open 27B. When a wrong answer costs a client, a diagnosis, or a legal position, a 25-point accuracy gap matters more than any aggregate index.</p> <p><strong>Long agentic chains are the second answer.</strong> Sonnet 4.6 reports 53.0 percent on Terminal-Bench Hard and 75.7 percent on τ²-Bench Telecom, which measure sustained tool use and multi-turn agent behavior. The open model’s card reports no comparable figures, and the absence is not encouraging.</p> <p><strong>The third answer is operational.</strong> A hosted API brings no driver updates, no quantization quirks, no fork of llama.cpp to track, and no rotated weight basis to get right. Someone else handles uptime and someone else gets paged at 3 AM.</p> <h3 id="the-question-worth-asking"> <a href="#the-question-worth-asking" title="The Question Worth Asking">The Question Worth Asking</a> <a href="#the-question-worth-asking" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Question Worth Asking">#</a> </h3> <p>So where does the premium tier stand outside the enterprise?</p> <p><strong>For knowledge-critical work, it still stands.</strong> Research, legal analysis, medical questions, financial modeling, and anything where a confident wrong answer is expensive. This is a genuine category, and the accuracy gap is a genuine reason to pay.</p> <p><strong>For generative work, the justification is thinning fast.</strong> Drafting, summarizing, refactoring code, reformatting data, classifying documents, and running automated pipelines are all tasks where output is verified before it is trusted. The accuracy gap costs little when a human or a test suite checks the result first. For those workloads, paying per token for a 30.1 index while a 33.7 index runs free on hardware you already own is a hard position to defend.</p> <p><strong>The decision has moved from capability to consequence.</strong> Two years ago the question was whether a local model was good enough to do the work at all. Today the question is what a mistake costs and how you would catch it.</p> <p><em>The enterprise premium buys reliability, compliance, and somebody else’s on-call rotation. Everyone else is paying for a difference which stops mattering the moment a test suite runs.</em></p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>A local 27B model now outscores Claude Sonnet 4.6 on the aggregate intelligence index</strong>, 33.7 against 30.1, and leads on coding, agentic tasks, long context, and graduate-level science reasoning.</li> <li><strong>Sonnet 4.6 still wins on factual accuracy</strong>, 40.9 percent against 15.6 percent on AA-Omniscience, which is the strongest remaining argument for the premium tier.</li> <li><strong>Ternary quantization is the change which makes this practical.</strong> Bonsai 2 27B runs the same 26.90B model in 5.53 GiB instead of 18 GB, and both are Apache 2.0.</li> <li><strong>Stock Ollama cannot run the ternary packs.</strong> They need Prism ML’s llama.cpp fork, and the F16 fallback silently produces incoherent output rather than failing.</li> <li><strong>Measured speed is 135 tokens per second decode</strong> on an RTX 5090, which outruns reading speed by a
