Prepare a Debian VM using a release listed in Docker’s installation documentation, establish backups, and configure resource allocations. Keep the original deployment available for rollback until the replacement passes its tests. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker’s Debian installation instructions"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/debian/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/debian/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker’s Debian installation instructions</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Inventory the Compose project</strong> from its working directory:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker compose config --quiet </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker compose config --images </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker compose config --volumes </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>--quiet</code></strong> validates the configuration without printing it. <strong><code>--images</code></strong> lists referenced images, while <strong><code>--volumes</code></strong> lists named volumes. These commands do not export application data or provide a complete bind-mount inventory. Review the Compose file and each container’s mounts as well. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker Compose config reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/config/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/config/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker Compose config reference</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Data or dependency</th> <th>Migration action</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Compose definitions</strong></td> <td>Transfer project files and retain the tested configuration</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Secrets and environment</strong></td> <td>Recreate required values through the chosen secret-management process</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Named volumes</strong></td> <td>Back up and restore their contents with application-consistent procedures</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Bind-mounted paths</strong></td> <td>Transfer or reconnect the actual source data and verify ownership</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Databases</strong></td> <td>Use the database’s supported backup/restore or quiesced-copy procedure</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Devices and shares</strong></td> <td>Re-establish access and test application behavior</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Ports and DNS</strong></td> <td>Stage the replacement address and plan the cutover</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Volumes</strong> outlive containers, but they do not migrate themselves. A Compose file names resources and defines services. Docker’s volume documentation describes separate backup and restore operations for persistent contents. Do not assume recreating the project restores its data. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker volume lifecycle and backups"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/volumes/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/volumes/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker volume lifecycle and backups</a> </span> </p> <p>Check <strong>Proxmox backup coverage</strong> separately. Its backup documentation excludes device and bind-mount contents from container backups. A successful backup of an LXC root filesystem therefore does not establish protection for every directory exposed inside it. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Proxmox backup documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/vzdump.adoc"> <a href="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/vzdump.adoc" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Proxmox backup documentation</a> </span> </p> <h3 id="check-storage-before-copying"> <a href="#check-storage-before-copying" title="Check Storage Before Copying">Check Storage Before Copying</a> <a href="#check-storage-before-copying" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Check Storage Before Copying">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Inspect Docker’s actual storage configuration</strong> on each Docker host:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>docker info </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>findmnt -T /var/lib/docker </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>findmnt</code></strong> identifies the filesystem containing the specified path. Replace <strong><code>/var/lib/docker</code></strong> if your daemon uses a different data root, and inspect containerd’s storage path when applicable. Docker documents a distinction between the containerd image store and classic storage drivers, with backend-specific requirements. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker storage-backend selection"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/select-storage-driver/"> <a href="https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/drivers/select-storage-driver/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Docker storage-backend selection</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Recreate images and restore application data</strong> using the chosen backend’s documented procedures. Copying a live Docker data directory between different storage arrangements introduces additional assumptions about metadata, mount state, and consistency. It is a different operation from backing up a stopped application’s data volume.</p> <h3 id="cut-over-with-rollback"> <a href="#cut-over-with-rollback" title="Cut Over With Rollback">Cut Over With Rollback</a> <a href="#cut-over-with-rollback" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Cut Over With Rollback">#</a> </h3> <ol> <li><strong>Rehearse restoration</strong> in the VM using separate addresses and test data where appropriate.</li> <li><strong>Stop production writes</strong> during the agreed outage window and take the final consistent backup.</li> <li><strong>Restore and validate</strong> application data, permissions, credentials, and required hardware access.</li> <li><strong>Switch service routing</strong> after the replacement passes application-specific checks.</li> <li><strong>Keep the original stopped</strong> while retaining its configuration and recovery data.</li> <li><strong>Document rollback handling</strong> for data written after cutover before restarting the old system.</li> </ol> <p>Avoid <strong>two active writers</strong> against the same database storage. A rollback involving new production data requires a plan for preserving or intentionally discarding those writes. Merely restarting an old container does not reconcile two diverging data histories.</p> <h2 id="test-more-than-uptime"> <a href="#test-more-than-uptime" title="Test More Than Uptime">Test More Than Uptime</a> <a href="#test-more-than-uptime" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Test More Than Uptime">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Acceptance tests</strong> should follow the service’s purpose. A green container status establishes a running process. A usable service also requires its data, network access, dependencies, and recovery behavior.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Test</th> <th>Evidence to retain</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Application function</strong></td> <td>A successful real transaction, query, or media operation</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Data completeness</strong></td> <td>Expected records, files, permissions, and recent changes</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Guest reboot</strong></td> <td>Services return without manual repair</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Backup restoration</strong></td> <td>The restored copy completes the same functional check</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Representative load</strong></td> <td>Latency, CPU, memory pressure, and storage behavior</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Maintenance rehearsal</strong></td> <td>A tested update and a usable recovery procedure</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Longer observation</strong></td> <td>Availability records spanning several previous failure intervals</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Worked decision:</strong> A camera service and an experimental downloader currently share one nested stack. Moving both into one VM improves kernel separation but preserves a shared guest-maintenance boundary. If camera availability is the priority, evaluate separate maintenance groups and resource limits, then test recording continuity during downloader updates.</p> <p><strong>Expected reasoning:</strong> The best placement follows the service dependency you need to isolate. Two VMs on one physical server still share its power, storage, and host kernel. If the requirement includes surviving the server’s outage, the design needs an additional independent system or an acceptable manual fallback.</p> <h2 id="create-your-decision-record"> <a href="#create-your-decision-record" title="Create Your Decision Record">Create Your Decision Record</a> <a href="#create-your-decision-record" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Create Your Decision Record">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Use measured evidence</strong> to choose a deployment and define when you will revisit it:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Service and household impact: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Current host / kernel / LXC / Docker versions: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Required GPU, device, and network access: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Measured memory, CPU, storage, and latency: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Known failure signature and recurrence interval: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Backup coverage and successful restore evidence: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Chosen deployment and reason: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Permitted outage window and recovery target: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Cutover and post-cutover data rollback procedure: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Acceptance tests and observation period: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Condition requiring another architecture review: </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Choose LXC nesting deliberately</strong> when its benefits justify the integration work and you have tested the recovery path. Choose a VM when a conventional Docker guest environment and a separate guest kernel simplify the service’s operation. Neither decision substitutes for backups, monitoring, and host maintenance.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Inventory one service</strong> first. Identify its persistent data, physical dependencies, failure symptoms, and recovery target. Rehearse a restore before deciding whether a migration is necessary.</p> <p>For <strong>related work</strong>, use the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Proxmox VE upgrade guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/proxmox-ve-8-to-9-upgrade-guide/"> <a href="/articles/proxmox-ve-8-to-9-upgrade-guide/" rel="follow me" >Proxmox VE upgrade guide</a> </span> for upgrade planning and the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Docker and Kubernetes security guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/how-to-secure-your-docker-and-kubernetes-environment/"> <a href="/articles/how-to-secure-your-docker-and-kubernetes-environment/" rel="follow me" >Docker and Kubernetes security guide</a> </span> for workload hardening. Keep architecture selection, upgrade execution, and incident diagnosis as distinct decisions with their own evidence.</p> <h2 id="sources-and-evidence"> <a href="#sources-and-evidence" title="Sources and Evidence">Sources and Evidence</a> <a href="#sources-and-evidence" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Sources and Evidence">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Research checked:</strong> September 16, 2026. item.title: Building a Privacy-Preserving AI Assistant for Meshtastic
item.description: A practical account of building a local AI assistant for Meshtastic, with private configuration, queued TCP access, retrieval tools, and a safer dashboard.
item.content:encoded: <p>Meshtastic provides text communication over low-power LoRa radios. Ollama provides a way to run an open model on local hardware. I combined the two into a small assistant that answers messages over a private mesh setup.</p> <h2 id="why-build-this"> <a href="#why-build-this" title="Why build this?">Why build this?</a> <a href="#why-build-this" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why build this?">#</a> </h2> <p>The goal was not to put a chatbot on a radio for its own sake. The goal was to make useful information available when normal internet services are unavailable, undesirable, or too dependent on a cloud account. A local assistant can keep questions, retrieved context, and responses inside the deployment while still using the mesh as a low-bandwidth interface.</p> <p>Power was part of that design goal. A useful node should be small enough to run on a Raspberry Pi 4, and efficient enough that a future deployment could pair it with a battery and a solar panel. Solar operation is an engineering target rather than a guaranteed property: the model, storage, radio, display, battery, panel, weather, and duty cycle all affect the energy budget. The practical design principle is to keep the services local, the answers concise, and the hardware modest so an off-grid version remains plausible.</p> <p>The project started as a simple Python bridge. It grew into a service with message filtering, source retrieval, a local control API, and a dashboard. The most useful lessons came from the failures. Each failure forced a clearer boundary between the radio connection, the model, and the web interface.</p> <h2 id="the-first-version-was-deliberately-small"> <a href="#the-first-version-was-deliberately-small" title="The first version was deliberately small">The first version was deliberately small</a> <a href="#the-first-version-was-deliberately-small" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The first version was deliberately small">#</a> </h2> <p>The first design had four parts:</p> <ul> <li>A Meshtastic node handled radio traffic.</li> <li>A Python process listened for text packets.</li> <li>Ollama generated a response on local hardware.</li> <li>The bridge sent the response back to the sender.</li> </ul> <p>The bridge used an OpenAI-compatible local endpoint. This kept the model interface simple and left the model choice in an environment file.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Meshtastic node -> TCP -> Python bridge -> local model </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> | </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> -> reply over Meshtastic </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The assistant answered direct messages first. This reduced noise while the message path was being tested.</p> <h2 id="channel-messages-needed-an-explicit-trigger"> <a href="#channel-messages-needed-an-explicit-trigger" title="Channel messages needed an explicit trigger">Channel messages needed an explicit trigger</a> <a href="#channel-messages-needed-an-explicit-trigger" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Channel messages needed an explicit trigger">#</a> </h2> <p>Answering every broadcast message would create noise and consume radio airtime. The bridge now ignores ordinary channel traffic. A channel request must start with a configurable prefix.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>!bot what is a checksum? </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>!bot weather <city or postal code> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>!bot news <topic> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>!bot wiki <subject> </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Direct messages do not need the prefix. The prefix rule keeps the assistant quiet during normal mesh conversations.</p> <p>The prefix lives in the private environment file:</p> <pre tabindex="0"><code class="language-dotenv" data-lang="dotenv">REPLY_TO_BROADCAST=true BOT_PREFIX=!bot </code></pre><h2 id="the-tcp-connection-became-the-main-design-problem"> <a href="#the-tcp-connection-became-the-main-design-problem" title="The TCP connection became the main design problem">The TCP connection became the main design problem</a> <a href="#the-tcp-connection-became-the-main-design-problem" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The TCP connection became the main design problem">#</a> </h2> <p>The Meshtastic node accepts one active client for its TCP API in this setup. The bridge owned the connection. The dashboard also tried to run the Meshtastic command-line client for status pages. Those two clients competed for the same socket.</p> <p>The result was confusing. The bridge process stayed active, yet its reader thread had stopped. A dashboard refresh was able to disconnect message handling. A node reconnect left a stale process behind.</p> <p>The fix was to make the bridge the only TCP owner.</p> <p>The bridge now exposes a small control API on the local machine. The dashboard asks the bridge for status, node data, and channel data. It never opens a second Meshtastic connection.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Dashboard -> local control API -> queued bridge operation -> Meshtastic TCP node </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> ^ </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Meshtastic TCP connection owned by the bridge </span></span></code></pre></div><p>A queue serializes control requests. A lock protects writes shared by the dashboard operations and bot replies. A heartbeat keeps idle TCP sessions open. A connection watchdog lets the service manager restart the bridge after a disconnect.</p> <p>This design also improves diagnosis. The dashboard reports connection state and queue depth without touching the radio session.</p> <h2 id="local-inference-required-practical-limits"> <a href="#local-inference-required-practical-limits" title="Local inference required practical limits">Local inference required practical limits</a> <a href="#local-inference-required-practical-limits" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Local inference required practical limits">#</a> </h2> <p>The target hardware has limited memory. The first model choice was too large for comfortable use. Prompt length, model loading, and radio-sized replies all affected response time.</p> <p>The final setup uses a smaller local model and a short reply limit. The bridge splits longer responses into multiple Meshtastic packets. The system also uses compressed memory swap and a conservative CPU setting on the host.</p> <p>These settings are not substitutes for a larger computer. They reduce avoidable pressure while keeping the service local.</p> <h2 id="retrieval-belongs-outside-the-system-prompt"> <a href="#retrieval-belongs-outside-the-system-prompt" title="Retrieval belongs outside the system prompt">Retrieval belongs outside the system prompt</a> <a href="#retrieval-belongs-outside-the-system-prompt" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Retrieval belongs outside the system prompt">#</a> </h2> <p>A small language model does not provide current weather or current news from its weights. The bridge added short, on-demand retrieval paths instead of downloading a full encyclopedia to the device.</p> <p>Supported requests include:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Wikipedia</strong> retrieves a matching page summary.</li> <li><strong>Weather</strong> retrieves a short current-condition line.</li> <li><strong>News</strong> reads recent titles from an RSS search feed.</li> </ul> <p>The retrieval source is placed in the user prompt as labeled context. The agent instructions tell the model to use the supplied source, state uncertainty, and avoid inventing article details.</p> <p>The bridge can also use a local Wikipedia RAG index. It is a small SQLite FTS5 database built from a curated JSONL export, so it does not require a resident vector database or a second embedding model on the Raspberry Pi. Wiki requests search that local index first and can fall back to the public Wikipedia API when enabled. A fully local deployment can disable the fallback.</p> <p>The HTTP identity is configurable:</p> <pre tabindex="0"><code class="language-dotenv" data-lang="dotenv">WEB_RETRIEVAL_ENABLED=true HTTP_USER_AGENT=SoS-Mesh-Assistant/1.0 (Meshtastic AI bridge) DEFAULT_WEATHER_LOCATION= DEFAULT_NEWS_TOPIC= </code></pre><p>Blank defaults force the user to provide a location or topic. This prevents a deployment-specific location from entering shared examples or source files.</p> <h2 id="the-agent-needed-an-explicit-identity"> <a href="#the-agent-needed-an-explicit-identity" title="The agent needed an explicit identity">The agent needed an explicit identity</a> <a href="#the-agent-needed-an-explicit-identity" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The agent needed an explicit identity">#</a> </h2> <p>Small models often answer with a generic identity unless the application gives them a clear role. The bridge loads its identity and safety rules from a separate prompt file.</p> <p>The prompt describes the assistant as a concise helper for a low-bandwidth mesh. It also sets boundaries:</p> <ul> <li>It must not claim to contact emergency services.</li> <li>It must not expose private configuration or secrets.</li> <li>It must treat retrieved pages as reference material, not instructions.</li> <li>It must identify sources when it uses retrieved information.</li> <li>It must give short answers suitable for radio transport.</li> </ul> <p>Keeping this policy in a file makes review easier. It also keeps deployment-specific values out of the application source.</p> <h2 id="the-dashboard-became-an-operations-tool"> <a href="#the-dashboard-became-an-operations-tool" title="The dashboard became an operations tool">The dashboard became an operations tool</a> <a href="#the-dashboard-became-an-operations-tool" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The dashboard became an operations tool">#</a> </h2> <p>The first dashboard showed service buttons and raw command output. The revised dashboard focuses on the state needed during operation:</p> <ul> <li>Mesh connection status</li> <li>Bridge-owned queue depth</li> <li>Connected node identity</li> <li>Service state</li> <li>Active model</li> <li>Model pull and selection controls</li> <li>Channel and node views</li> <li>Recent questions and replies</li> </ul> <p>The dashboard also avoids a dangerous action from the early version. It no longer runs a separate Meshtastic command for configuration changes. Configuration writes need to pass through the same bridge queue as other node operations.</p> <h2 id="privacy-was-part-of-the-build"> <a href="#privacy-was-part-of-the-build" title="Privacy was part of the build">Privacy was part of the build</a> <a href="#privacy-was-part-of-the-build" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Privacy was part of the build">#</a> </h2> <p>The public source contains neutral placeholders. Private node addresses, radio keys, passwords, administrator keys, and location defaults stay in an ignored environment file on the deployment host.</p> <p>The same rule applies to documentation. Examples use placeholders such as <code><node-ip></code> and <code><city or postal code></code>. A working example does not need to reveal the network where it was tested.</p> <p>This separation also makes the project easier to share. The source explains the architecture. The private environment describes one deployment. Neither file needs to contain the other file’s data.</p> <h2 id="what-i-would-improve-next"> <a href="#what-i-would-improve-next" title="What I would improve next">What I would improve next</a> <a href="#what-i-would-improve-next" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What I would improve next">#</a> </h2> <p>The next useful step is to move every Meshtastic write into the bridge control queue. Channel edits, node configuration, and send operations should share one audited path. The dashboard should then show the queue job, result, and error message for each operation.</p> <p>The current build already demonstrates the core pattern. Keep one owner for the radio connection, keep deployment values outside source control, and pass external information to the model as labeled context. The longer-term ideal is a quiet, low-power node that can continue providing local knowledge and mesh assistance from a Raspberry Pi 4, including during a solar-powered deployment.</p> <p>Meshtastic documentation: <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Meshtastic introduction"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://meshtastic.org/docs/"> <a href="https://meshtastic.org/docs/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Meshtastic introduction</a> </span> </p> <p>Local model runtime: <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Ollama"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://ollama.com/"> <a href="https://ollama.com/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Ollama</a> </span> </p> <p>Wikipedia API reference: <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Wikipedia REST API page summary"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/summary/Wikipedia"> <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/summary/Wikipedia" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Wikipedia REST API page summary</a> </span> </p> <p>Source code: <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Meshtastic AI Bridge on GitHub"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/simeononsecurity/meshtastic-ai-bridge"> <a href="https://github.com/simeononsecurity/meshtastic-ai-bridge" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Meshtastic AI Bridge on GitHub</a> </span> </p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Module 1: Red Team Methodology
item.description: The seven-phase red team methodology: preparation, intelligence, reconnaissance, access, post exploitation, cleanup and backout, and reporting, with the judgment behind each.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="-return-to-the-red-team-course"> <a href="#-return-to-the-red-team-course" title=" ← Return to the Red Team Course "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Red Team Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course-start/"> <a href="/red-team-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Red Team Course</a> </span> </a> <a href="#-return-to-the-red-team-course" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" ← Return to the Red Team Course ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>Red team methodology</strong> connects an agreed business question to a controlled test and evidence the customer is able to use. This course uses six phases to organize the work, with feedback between phases as observations change the plan. Your outcome is an evidence-backed conclusion, an explained limit, and a verified restoration record.</p> <p><em>Allow 25 minutes for reading and 30 minutes for the tabletop exercise. No attack tooling is required for this module.</em></p> <h2 id="learning-outcomes"> <a href="#learning-outcomes" title="Learning Outcomes">Learning Outcomes</a> <a href="#learning-outcomes" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Learning Outcomes">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Recall the phases:</strong> place a technique within a larger operation.</li> <li><strong>Explain the objective:</strong> distinguish access, business impact, and assessment evidence.</li> <li><strong>Apply a planning method:</strong> connect an approved action to a specific observation.</li> <li><strong>Evaluate a result:</strong> distinguish prevention, missing telemetry, and insufficient evidence.</li> <li><strong>Create a test plan:</strong> define entry conditions, stopping points, cleanup, and acceptance criteria.</li> </ul> <h2 id="the-six-phases"> <a href="#the-six-phases" title="The Six Phases">The Six Phases</a> <a href="#the-six-phases" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Six Phases">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The seven-phase model</strong> is this course’s organizing convention. It is not the MITRE ATT&CK matrix, an official maturity score, or a guarantee of one correct sequence. An operation often returns to reconnaissance after a new observation, and some tests finish without persistence or a domain-controller objective.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Phase</th> <th>Main question</th> <th>Deliverable</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Mission preparation</strong></td> <td>What is authorized and ready?</td> <td>Scope, test conditions, contacts, and infrastructure inventory</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Open-source intelligence</strong></td> <td>What does public information support?</td> <td>Attributed observations with confidence and collection dates</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Active reconnaissance</strong></td> <td>What does interaction with the approved environment reveal?</td> <td>A bounded target and dependency map</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Target exploitation</strong></td> <td>Does the selected route produce the intended test condition?</td> <td>Reproducible evidence of success, prevention, or a limit</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Post exploitation</strong></td> <td>Which approved objective follows from the obtained context?</td> <td>An access path and its observed effects</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cleanup and backout</strong></td> <td>What must be removed or restored?</td> <td>Artifact ledger, backout actions, and baseline verification</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Mission objective and reporting</strong></td> <td>What did the assessment prove?</td> <td>Findings, restoration evidence, and remediation priorities</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Cleanup, backout, and reporting begin during preparation.</strong> They are not tasks postponed until the final day. An operation lacking an artifact register, original-state record, or timestamps is difficult to explain even when the technical action succeeds.</p> <h2 id="objectives-before-techniques"> <a href="#objectives-before-techniques" title="Objectives Before Techniques">Objectives Before Techniques</a> <a href="#objectives-before-techniques" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Objectives Before Techniques">#</a> </h2> <p>A <strong>mission objective</strong> states the question the assessment is intended to answer. “Obtain administrator access” is incomplete unless it explains which business or control outcome the access tests. A customer might instead need evidence about segregation between application roles or the ability to recognize one defined behavior.</p> <p><strong>Illustrative objective:</strong> Determine whether a synthetic finance user is permitted to read a restricted sample report outside their role. The sample report contains no real financial data. Success means the test establishes an access-control result and collects enough evidence to reproduce the conclusion.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Weak objective</th> <th>More useful formulation</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Get a shell</strong></td> <td>Determine whether the approved entry route reaches the designated lab execution context</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Become domain admin</strong></td> <td>Evaluate the named privilege boundary supporting the agreed business scenario</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Avoid detection</strong></td> <td>Measure which approved behaviors produce telemetry, alerts, and analyst action</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Exfiltrate data</strong></td> <td>Demonstrate the approved data path using a designated synthetic marker and transfer limit</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>An objective also defines when to stop.</strong> If a sample-file read answers the question, copying an entire share adds data exposure without improving the finding. The test plan should identify the minimum proof before an operator reaches the resource.</p> <h2 id="use-attck-precisely"> <a href="#use-attck-precisely" title="Use ATT&CK Precisely">Use ATT&CK Precisely</a> <a href="#use-attck-precisely" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Use ATT&CK Precisely">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>MITRE ATT&CK</strong> provides a vocabulary for adversary behavior. A tactic describes an adversary goal, while a technique describes behavior supporting a goal. Map a specific observation to a technique when the evidence supports it, then retain the actual procedure and environment details alongside the mapping. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="MITRE guidance on adversary emulation and red teaming"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://attack.mitre.org/resources/get-started/adversary-emulation-and-red-teaming/"> <a href="https://attack.mitre.org/resources/get-started/adversary-emulation-and-red-teaming/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >MITRE guidance on adversary emulation and red teaming</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>A technique identifier is not a test result.</strong> Listing an identifier does not establish whether an action executed, whether a sensor recorded it, or whether an analyst understood it. Different implementations of a related behavior also exercise different prerequisites and telemetry.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/objective-evidence-review-loop.webp", "caption": "Diagram linking an assessment objective to an approved test, collected evidence, and a review decision", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-09-23 04:19:53.681751676 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b499.239452007", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-09-23 04:19:53.681751676 +0000 UTC m=+499.239452007"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/objective-evidence-review-loop.webp" alt="Diagram linking an assessment objective to an approved test, collected evidence, and a review decision"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>Every test needs a question, a bounded action, and evidence supporting its conclusion</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <h2 id="preparation-and-scope"> <a href="#preparation-and-scope" title="Preparation and Scope">Preparation and Scope</a> <a href="#preparation-and-scope" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Preparation and Scope">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Mission preparation</strong> establishes the assets, actions, identities, and time windows included in the exercise. It also records exclusions, data-handling rules, operational contacts, and the restoration process. NIST’s assessment guidance provides a planning reference for these decisions. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="NIST SP 800-115"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/115/final"> <a href="https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/115/final" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >NIST SP 800-115</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Deconfliction</strong> is the process for comparing suspicious activity with the team’s authorized actions. A matching source address alone is weak evidence. Use timestamps, action identifiers, hosts, accounts, and operator records to distinguish the exercise from an unrelated incident.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Planning item</th> <th>Example decision</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Target boundary</strong></td> <td>Only the named lab application and two test accounts</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Permitted action</strong></td> <td>Attempt a read of the designated synthetic report</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Stop condition</strong></td> <td>An unrelated production record appears</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Contact</strong></td> <td>Named exercise controller and a tested backup channel</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Restoration</strong></td> <td>Remove test grants and verify the baseline role assignments</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Scope changes require a recorded decision.</strong> A newly reachable system or interesting credential is an observation, not an extension of the approved target list. Bring the observation to the exercise controller before treating it as another test step.</p> <h2 id="osint-and-active-reconnaissance"> <a href="#osint-and-active-reconnaissance" title="OSINT and Active Reconnaissance">OSINT and Active Reconnaissance</a> <a href="#osint-and-active-reconnaissance" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="OSINT and Active Reconnaissance">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Open-source intelligence (OSINT)</strong> uses publicly available information. Its collection method determines whether it touches customer-controlled infrastructure. Reading an archived page differs from browsing the customer’s live site, and public content still produces access logs when requested directly.</p> <p><strong>Active reconnaissance</strong> deliberately interacts with a target to answer a specific question. The important distinction is the collection path and the resulting evidence, not an absolute claim about generating zero alerts. Document both third-party sources and direct interactions.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Collection</th> <th>Likely observation point</th> <th>Limitation</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Third-party archive</strong></td> <td>Archive provider</td> <td>Historical content might be stale</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Public registration record</strong></td> <td>Registry or lookup provider</td> <td>Ownership does not establish test authorization</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Live customer webpage</strong></td> <td>Customer web or proxy logs</td> <td>Public access is still direct interaction</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Approved service probe</strong></td> <td>Target network and service logs</td> <td>A response establishes only the tested condition</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Reconnaissance produces hypotheses.</strong> A banner suggesting an older product version is a lead to validate, not proof of an exploitable vulnerability. A missing response likewise does not prove a host is absent.</p> <h2 id="exploitation-and-post-exploitation"> <a href="#exploitation-and-post-exploitation" title="Exploitation and Post Exploitation">Exploitation and Post Exploitation</a> <a href="#exploitation-and-post-exploitation" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Exploitation and Post Exploitation">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Target exploitation</strong> tests a selected route within the agreed conditions. Select the route because it answers the objective and fits the risk constraints. There is no requirement to demonstrate every possible weakness or to persist after every successful entry.</p> <p><strong>Post exploitation</strong> evaluates the context obtained after access. Identity, privilege, reachable resources, and dependencies determine which approved next step is meaningful. Extra persistence or lateral movement adds work and artifacts, so it needs a reason tied to the scenario.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Result</th> <th>Useful next decision</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Route prevented</strong></td> <td>Preserve prevention evidence and determine whether another route is part of scope</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Low-privilege access obtained</strong></td> <td>Record the context and test the permitted objective</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Objective already satisfied</strong></td> <td>Stop expansion and validate evidence and restoration</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Unexpected sensitive access</strong></td> <td>Pause and use the agreed deconfliction channel</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A domain controller is one possible dependency</strong>, not the destination of every operation. The assessment might finish at a file-server permission boundary or a cloud application’s role check. Explain the business significance of the result instead of treating domain control as a universal score.</p> <h2 id="supplemental-video"> <a href="#supplemental-video" title="Supplemental Video">Supplemental Video</a> <a href="#supplemental-video" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Supplemental Video">#</a> </h2> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { if (typeof yieldToMain === 'function') { yieldToMain(loadLiteYouTubeScript, "user-visible"); } else { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); } }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style><div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/VideoObject http://schema.org/LearningResource" style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Adversary Emulation: Generating MITRE ATT&CK Technique Sequences"> <meta itemprop="description" content="YouTube Video"> <meta itemprop="thumbnailUrl" content="https://img.youtube.com/vi/tvQbh0bawEM/maxresdefault.jpg"> <meta itemprop="contentUrl" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tvQbh0bawEM"> <meta itemprop="learningResourceType" content="Concept Overview"> <meta itemprop="educationalLevel" content="High school (US)"> <lite-youtube videoid="tvQbh0bawEM" videotitle="Adversary Emulation: Generating MITRE ATT&CK Technique Sequences" videoplay="" nocookie posterloading="lazy" loading="lazy" params=""> <noscript> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tvQbh0bawEM" class="lite-youtube-fallback" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="Adversary Emulation: Generating MITRE ATT&CK Technique Sequences"> <span class="lyt-visually-hidden"></span> </a> </noscript> </lite-youtube> </div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": ["VideoObject", "LearningResource"], "name": "Adversary Emulation: Generating MITRE ATT\u0026CK Technique Sequences", "description": "YouTube Video", "thumbnailUrl": ["https:\/\/img.youtube.com\/vi\/tvQbh0bawEM\/maxresdefault.jpg"], "contentUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tvQbh0bawEM", "learningResourceType": "Concept Overview", "educationalLevel": "High school (US)" } </script> <p><strong>Watch:</strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Adversary Emulation: Generating MITRE ATT&CK Technique Sequences"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tvQbh0bawEM"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tvQbh0bawEM" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Adversary Emulation: Generating MITRE ATT&CK Technique Sequences</a> </span> , presented by Martin Eian and published by FIRST. The presentation examines dependencies between techniques when assembling an emulation sequence. Use it to assess why a list of behaviors needs an execution plan.</p> <p><strong>Viewing task:</strong> Pick two behaviors from a fictional scenario and write the prerequisite connecting them. Then identify one condition under which the second behavior would be irrelevant. Compare the dependency with the objective instead of assuming a longer sequence is a better test.</p> <h2 id="evidence-has-several-stages"> <a href="#evidence-has-several-stages" title="Evidence Has Several Stages">Evidence Has Several Stages</a> <a href="#evidence-has-several-stages" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Evidence Has Several Stages">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Execution, collection, alerting, and response</strong> are different outcomes. A successful test action might produce an event without generating an alert. An alert might exist without reaching an analyst inside the evaluation window. Report each observed stage separately.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Stage</th> <th>Evidence needed</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Action executed</strong></td> <td>Operator record and observed target-side result</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Telemetry collected</strong></td> <td>Relevant event present at the expected sensor or collector</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Detection generated</strong></td> <td>Alert tied to the test’s entity and time</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Analyst response</strong></td> <td>Case activity showing interpretation and an action</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Restoration verified</strong></td> <td>Comparison against the agreed baseline</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>An empty search is not a detection verdict.</strong> The event might be missing because logging was disabled, collection failed, timestamps differ, or the search selected the wrong host. Resolve these possibilities before classifying a control gap.</p> <p><strong>Illustrative reasoning:</strong> A file-access exercise succeeds at 10:05 UTC. The operator has a screenshot, but the analyst searches local time and finds no event. The first follow-up is time and collection correlation, not a claim of undetected access.</p> <h2 id="cleanup-and-backout"> <a href="#cleanup-and-backout" title="Cleanup and Backout">Cleanup and Backout</a> <a href="#cleanup-and-backout" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Cleanup and Backout">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Cleanup</strong> removes artifacts owned by the exercise. <strong>Backout</strong> returns modified systems to the agreed baseline. The two actions overlap, but they are not identical. A newly created test value might be removed, while a pre-existing permission change needs its recorded original value restored.</p> <p><strong>Plan the backout before the first state change.</strong> Record the owner, original value, affected process, trigger, evidence location, and verification step. Preserve customer logs and assessment evidence according to the engagement agreement. Backout does not mean erasing the record of what happened.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Backout item</th> <th>Required evidence</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Created artifact</strong></td> <td>Ownership record, removal result, and absence check</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Modified setting</strong></td> <td>Original value, narrow restoration, and comparison</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Running process</strong></td> <td>Process owner, stop action, and later state</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Service or task</strong></td> <td>Configuration baseline, state, and trigger retest</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Customer evidence</strong></td> <td>Retention decision and report reference</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Backout completion is a finding</strong>, not an assumption. Mark each item verified, unresolved, or retained by agreement. If another administrator changed the same object, pause the reversal and use the named owner to resolve the conflict.</p> <p><strong>Exercise:</strong> Add a cleanup and backout section to the synthetic finance-report test card. List one created artifact, one modified setting, one running process, and the evidence proving each final state. State the condition preventing backout from proceeding safely.</p> <p><strong>Expected reasoning:</strong> The artifact register determines ownership. The original-state record determines restoration. A process check determines whether the removed trigger left an existing instance running. A conflict with a later administrator change requires owner review rather than an automatic overwrite.</p> <h2 id="design-one-bounded-test"> <a href="#design-one-bounded-test" title="Design One Bounded Test">Design One Bounded Test</a> <a href="#design-one-bounded-test" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Design One Bounded Test">#</a> </h2> <p>Use this <strong>test-card template</strong> before a tabletop or lab exercise:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Business question: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Approved assets and identities: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Required starting context: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Behavior and ATT&CK mapping, if justified: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Permitted action and maximum scope: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Expected operator-side evidence: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Expected defender-side observation: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Stop conditions and controller contact: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Restoration steps and verification: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Observed result, limitations, and next decision: </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Micro emulation plans</strong> provide examples of narrowly scoped tests organized around specific behaviors. Their value is repeatability and an explicit relationship between action and observation. Adapt the idea to the customer question rather than treating a public plan as approval to run it. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="MITRE Center for Threat-Informed Defense project"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://ctid.mitre.org/projects/micro-emulation-plans/"> <a href="https://ctid.mitre.org/projects/micro-emulation-plans/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >MITRE Center for Threat-Informed Defense project</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Exercise:</strong> Create a card for the synthetic finance-report scenario. Include an authorized reader and a restricted reader, the exact sample resource, a collection window, and the restoration check. Record what would establish a permission problem and what would leave the result inconclusive.</p> <h2 id="evaluate-your-test-card"> <a href="#evaluate-your-test-card" title="Evaluate Your Test Card">Evaluate Your Test Card</a> <a href="#evaluate-your-test-card" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Evaluate Your Test Card">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Expected reasoning:</strong> The authorized reader establishes a baseline for the resource’s availability. The restricted reader tests the intended access boundary. A successful unauthorized read supports the access-control finding, while a timeout requires investigation before it supports any permission conclusion.</p> <p><strong>Improve the plan</strong> by adding one controlled variation. For example, repeat the same read after correcting the sample folder permission. Keep the identities, resource, and collection method stable so the comparison answers a clear question.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Review question</th> <th>A useful answer contains</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>What is being tested?</strong></td> <td>A named business or control boundary</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>What changes?</strong></td> <td>One explicit action or configuration difference</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>What proves the result?</strong></td> <td>Evidence from the relevant layer</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>What ends the test?</strong></td> <td>A success condition, limit, or stop rule</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>What remains afterward?</strong></td> <td>An artifact inventory and verified baseline</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="self-check"> <a href="#self-check" title="Self-Check">Self-Check</a> <a href="#self-check" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Self-Check">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li><strong>Seven phases:</strong> Which phases repeat after new evidence appears?</li> <li><strong>OSINT:</strong> Why does publicly available information not imply zero interaction?</li> <li><strong>ATT&CK:</strong> What does a technique identifier leave unspecified?</li> <li><strong>Post exploitation:</strong> When is additional persistence unnecessary?</li> <li><strong>Negative result:</strong> What must you examine before calling an action undetected?</li> </ol> <p><strong>Answer key:</strong> Reconnaissance and planning repeat as the situation changes. Public resources still have collection paths and access logs. ATT&CK identifiers leave procedure, prerequisites, and actual test results to document.</p> <p><strong>Operation decisions:</strong> Persistence is unnecessary when the objective does not require it. An undetected-action claim needs verified execution, appropriate collection, a valid search, and a defined observation window. Cleanup and backout need their own final-state evidence.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Keep your test card</strong> and refine its infrastructure and deconfliction requirements in <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Module 2: Mission Preparation and Infrastructure"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course/mission-preparation-and-infrastructure/"> <a href="/red-team-course/mission-preparation-and-infrastructure/" rel="follow me" >Module 2: Mission Preparation and Infrastructure</a> </span> </strong>. Return to the <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="course hub"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course-start/"> <a href="/red-team-course-start/" rel="follow me" >course hub</a> </span> </strong> for the module sequence.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Module 10: Initial Access: Phishing and Delivery
item.description: Distinguish phishing delivery, interaction, execution, and access. Interpret campaign metrics, modern Office controls, and Windows architecture with worked examples.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="-return-to-the-red-team-course"> <a href="#-return-to-the-red-team-course" title=" ← Return to the Red Team Course "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Red Team Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course-start/"> <a href="/red-team-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Red Team Course</a> </span> </a> <a href="#-return-to-the-red-team-course" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" ← Return to the Red Team Course ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>Initial access</strong> is the establishment of a usable starting context for an assessment. A delivered message, a clicked link, and code execution represent different outcomes. Your test should identify which boundary it examines and collect evidence appropriate to the tested boundary.</p> <p><em>Allow about 20 minutes, plus time to design the simulation record. The worked examples use synthetic events and require no messages sent to real recipients.</em></p> <h2 id="what-you-will-learn"> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" title="What You Will Learn">What You Will Learn</a> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What You Will Learn">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Distinguish</strong> delivery, interaction, execution, and communication outcomes.</li> <li><strong>Explain</strong> how email, document, identity, and endpoint controls affect an access path.</li> <li><strong>Analyze</strong> a synthetic campaign’s rates and ambiguous events.</li> <li><strong>Evaluate</strong> whether two simulations support a fair comparison.</li> <li><strong>Create</strong> a bounded initial-access test specification and handover record.</li> </ul> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Term</th> <th>Meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Delivery</strong></td> <td>A message or artifact reaches the specified destination</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Interaction</strong></td> <td>A recorded action such as following a link</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Execution</strong></td> <td>Instructions run in an identified process and security context</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Foothold</strong></td> <td>Usable access within the assessment’s permitted scope</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Mark of the Web</strong></td> <td>Windows zone information associated with some downloaded files</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Simulation artifact</strong></td> <td>Harmless material used to exercise an agreed control or behavior</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="choose-the-access-boundary"> <a href="#choose-the-access-boundary" title="Choose the Access Boundary">Choose the Access Boundary</a> <a href="#choose-the-access-boundary" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Choose the Access Boundary">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Phishing</strong> is one initial-access technique, not a universally reliable route. Its outcome depends on the scenario, delivery path, controls, and user context. An assessment might instead examine a public application boundary or begin from a deliberately supplied test account.</p> <p><strong>Remote code execution</strong> means an input causes instructions to run remotely. An upload feature alone does not establish this condition. File validation, storage location, server configuration, execution permissions, and how the uploaded content is handled determine the effect.</p> <p><strong>A web shell</strong> is server-side code exposing a command interface through a web application. Its presence is an execution and access concern, not the ordinary outcome of every uploaded document. Keep a suspected upload weakness separate from proof of server-side execution. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Read MITRE ATT&CK’s web-shell description"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1505/003/"> <a href="https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1505/003/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Read MITRE ATT&CK’s web-shell description</a> </span> .</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Proposed test</th> <th>Boundary examined</th> <th>Minimal useful proof</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Mail simulation</strong></td> <td>Delivery and recipient response</td> <td>Correlated message and interaction records</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Document-control test</strong></td> <td>Opening and execution policy</td> <td>Policy result for an inert test artifact</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Application assessment</strong></td> <td>Input handling and authorization</td> <td>Bounded reproducible behavior</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Assumed-access exercise</strong></td> <td>Controls after a defined starting point</td> <td>Documented supplied identity and privileges</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="trace-the-delivery-chain"> <a href="#trace-the-delivery-chain" title="Trace the Delivery Chain">Trace the Delivery Chain</a> <a href="#trace-the-delivery-chain" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Trace the Delivery Chain">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A message’s lifecycle</strong> crosses several independent controls. Sending infrastructure, receiving mail systems, clients, browsers, endpoint policy, and network access each contribute a possible outcome. Name the stage where the observation occurred instead of reporting every failure as “phishing blocked.”</p> <p><strong>Human interaction</strong> also needs interpretation. A tracking request does not necessarily establish a deliberate click by the recipient. Microsoft documents false positives caused by security applications and automated message inspection, including interactions with forwarded simulation messages. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Read the simulation FAQ"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/attack-simulation-training-faq"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/attack-simulation-training-faq" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Read the simulation FAQ</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Execution and callback evidence</strong> are separate again. Even an authorized test program which starts successfully might fail to reach its reporting endpoint. Use the task-state distinctions from <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Module 5"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course/command-and-control-operations/"> <a href="/red-team-course/command-and-control-operations/" rel="follow me" >Module 5</a> </span> when recording these outcomes.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/delivery-interaction-execution-boundaries.webp", "caption": "Four connected boxes distinguish message delivery, interpreted interaction, endpoint execution, and confirmed usable assessment access", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-09-23 04:19:53.686427742 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b499.244128063", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-09-23 04:19:53.686427742 +0000 UTC m=+499.244128063"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/delivery-interaction-execution-boundaries.webp" alt="Four connected boxes distinguish message delivery, interpreted interaction, endpoint execution, and confirmed usable assessment access"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>Each transition needs evidence beyond success at the previous stage</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <h2 id="set-up-the-measurement"> <a href="#set-up-the-measurement" title="Set Up the Measurement">Set Up the Measurement</a> <a href="#set-up-the-measurement" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Set Up the Measurement">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Gophish campaign configuration</strong> combines recipients, an email template, a landing page, a sending profile, and scheduling details. Its campaign records track events for analysis. Review the platform’s event definitions before assigning stronger meanings to the displayed labels. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Read the Gophish campaign documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.getgophish.com/user-guide/documentation/campaigns"> <a href="https://docs.getgophish.com/user-guide/documentation/campaigns" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Read the Gophish campaign documentation</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>A sending profile</strong> defines the approved sending service and related settings. It does not inherently require impersonating an unrelated organization. A landing page also need not collect credentials, so choose an inert completion page when a link-following measurement meets the objective.</p> <p><strong>Training and control assessment</strong> differ in purpose. An awareness exercise measures recognition, reporting, and learning under defined conditions. A technical assessment measures whether the delivery and execution controls work along an agreed path, so changes which permit training delivery alter the technical test.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Measurement</th> <th>Useful evidence</th> <th>Limitation</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Delivered</strong></td> <td>Receiving-system or platform delivery record</td> <td>Does not prove the recipient read it</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Opened</strong></td> <td>Platform-defined observation</td> <td>Image handling and client behavior affect it</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Clicked</strong></td> <td>Correlated interaction record</td> <td>Automated inspection needs review</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Reported</strong></td> <td>User-reporting workflow event</td> <td>Platform coverage and timing differ</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Executed</strong></td> <td>Endpoint-side process and result evidence</td> <td>Does not prove usable remote access</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="account-for-document-controls"> <a href="#account-for-document-controls" title="Account for Document Controls">Account for Document Controls</a> <a href="#account-for-document-controls" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Account for Document Controls">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Office macro behavior</strong> depends on application version, file origin, and policy. Microsoft’s current guidance documents default blocking of macros from internet-sourced files in affected Office applications. An older demonstration of an attachment launching code is insufficient evidence of behavior on a current managed device. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Read Microsoft’s macro-blocking guidance"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365-apps/security/internet-macros-blocked"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365-apps/security/internet-macros-blocked" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Read Microsoft’s macro-blocking guidance</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Record the environment</strong> before testing a document control. Include the application build, delivery method, relevant policy, and observed warning or block. A harmless file with no executable content tests delivery or opening, but not whether a malicious macro would have executed.</p> <p><strong>Do not change the tested control mid-run</strong> merely to obtain a desired outcome. If the approved exercise needs an exception for training delivery, record the exception and narrow the conclusion accordingly. An intentionally permitted path does not establish the baseline control would have allowed it.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Test condition</th> <th>Conclusion boundary</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Inert attachment opens</strong></td> <td>File delivery and opening worked</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Macro policy blocks a test document</strong></td> <td>The observed policy prevented the tested execution path</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Training delivery exception enabled</strong></td> <td>Result applies to the exception configuration</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Different Office build used</strong></td> <td>Comparison needs a version qualification</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="work-through-campaign-rates"> <a href="#work-through-campaign-rates" title="Work Through Campaign Rates">Work Through Campaign Rates</a> <a href="#work-through-campaign-rates" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Work Through Campaign Rates">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Illustrative scenario:</strong> a simulation targets 100 approved training accounts. Ten messages fail delivery. Among the 90 delivered messages, the platform records 18 unique accounts with click events, and review identifies six of those accounts as automation-only events. Fifteen accounts report the message through the training workflow.</p> <p><strong>Calculate the rates</strong> before interpreting them. Use delivered accounts as the denominator for this exercise and count each account once per metric. The reporting and clicking groups might overlap, so do not add them as mutually exclusive categories.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Metric</th> <th>Calculation</th> <th>Result</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Delivery rate</strong></td> <td>90 / 100</td> <td>90%</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Raw recorded-click rate</strong></td> <td>18 / 90</td> <td>20%</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Reviewed user-click rate</strong></td> <td>12 / 90</td> <td>About 13.3%</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Reporting rate</strong></td> <td>15 / 90</td> <td>About 16.7%</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Expected reasoning:</strong> the raw click count overstates the reviewed user count in this synthetic dataset. Keep both values and document the review criteria rather than silently editing history. None of these rates establishes a compromised endpoint or a captured credential.</p> <p><strong>A stronger report</strong> includes delivery failures, ambiguous events, reporting delay, and the exact denominator. Microsoft provides several simulation and training reports with defined metrics, so use the relevant report’s definitions when interpreting a real export. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Read the reporting documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/attack-simulation-training-insights"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-office-365/attack-simulation-training-insights" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Read the reporting documentation</a> </span> .</p> <h2 id="compare-difficulty-fairly"> <a href="#compare-difficulty-fairly" title="Compare Difficulty Fairly">Compare Difficulty Fairly</a> <a href="#compare-difficulty-fairly" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Compare Difficulty Fairly">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Different messages create different tasks</strong> for recipients. An obviously unrelated request and a plausible work-context message are not equivalent challenges. A lower click rate on the easier message does not establish improved recognition across all phishing scenarios.</p> <p><strong>The NIST Phish Scale</strong> provides a method for rating human phishing-detection difficulty. It considers message cues and premise alignment with the audience. Use its documented method alongside outcome metrics when comparing exercises. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Read the NIST Phish Scale User Guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.nist.gov/publications/nist-phish-scale-user-guide"> <a href="https://www.nist.gov/publications/nist-phish-scale-user-guide" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Read the NIST Phish Scale User Guide</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Compare like conditions</strong> wherever possible. Record audience, message difficulty, reporting tools, delivery exceptions, timing, and any preceding training. If several conditions changed, describe the combined result and avoid attributing it to one cause.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Comparison difference</th> <th>Possible effect</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>New recipient group</strong></td> <td>Different role context and prior experience</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Different message premise</strong></td> <td>Different detection difficulty</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Delivery-policy exception</strong></td> <td>Different exposure to the technical controls</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Automated-click filtering</strong></td> <td>Different measurement rather than changed behavior</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="inspect-architecture-context"> <a href="#inspect-architecture-context" title="Inspect Architecture Context">Inspect Architecture Context</a> <a href="#inspect-architecture-context" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Inspect Architecture Context">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Windows process architecture</strong> matters when interpreting a subsequent test. Starting a service or using a particular operator command does not automatically imply a 32-bit process. Verify the actual process, operating system, and artifact architecture instead of inferring them from the workflow’s name.</p> <p><strong>WOW64 filesystem redirection</strong> affects many accesses from 32-bit processes to the Windows system directory on 64-bit Windows. The <strong><code>Sysnative</code></strong> alias lets a 32-bit application address the native system directory. It is not an ordinary physical directory or a universal path for 64-bit applications. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Read Microsoft’s filesystem-redirector documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/winprog64/file-system-redirector"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/winprog64/file-system-redirector" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Read Microsoft’s filesystem-redirector documentation</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>A read-only PowerShell check</strong> distinguishes the current shell process from the operating system. Run it inside the shell whose context you are examining. It says nothing about the architecture of an unrelated application.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-powershell" data-lang="powershell"><span style="display:flex;"><span>[<span style="color:#66d9ef">Environment</span>]::Is64BitOperatingSystem </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>[<span style="color:#66d9ef">Environment</span>]::Is64BitProcess </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Interpret the booleans</strong> in order. A true OS result and false process result indicate a 32-bit PowerShell process on a 64-bit operating system. Two true results indicate a 64-bit process on a 64-bit OS. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Read the .NET process-architecture property"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.environment.is64bitprocess?view=net-9.0"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.environment.is64bitprocess?view=net-9.0" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Read the .NET process-architecture property</a> </span> .</p> <h2 id="handle-unexpected-recipients"> <a href="#handle-unexpected-recipients" title="Handle Unexpected Recipients">Handle Unexpected Recipients</a> <a href="#handle-unexpected-recipients" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Handle Unexpected Recipients">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Forwarding and remote reading</strong> introduce scope uncertainty. A simulation URL tied to one recipient might be fetched from another device or by another person. Treat the correlation token as a record key, not proof of the operator’s identity or device ownership.</p> <p><strong>An unexpected interaction</strong> should trigger the agreed containment and review process. Stop any dependent assessment action, retain the minimal event evidence, and reconcile the event with the campaign owner.
