Record the resolver and query result, then compare them with the intended lab configuration.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/domain-access-dependency-map.webp", "caption": "Diagram connecting DNS service location, domain authentication, resource authorization, and evidence from each stage", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-09-23 04:19:53.738135895 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b499.295836216", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-09-23 04:19:53.738135895 +0000 UTC m=+499.295836216"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/domain-access-dependency-map.webp" alt="Diagram connecting DNS service location, domain authentication, resource authorization, and evidence from each stage"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>Reachability, authentication, and permission require separate evidence</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <h2 id="groups-and-effective-access"> <a href="#groups-and-effective-access" title="Groups and Effective Access">Groups and Effective Access</a> <a href="#groups-and-effective-access" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Groups and Effective Access">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Security groups</strong> support permission assignments to collections of accounts and other groups. Distribution groups serve a different purpose and are not security principals for permission assignment. Group scope constrains valid membership and where permissions apply. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft security-group documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/manage/understand-security-groups"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/manage/understand-security-groups" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft security-group documentation</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Group names are not permission evidence.</strong> A group called Finance Admins needs an actual rights assignment or resource permission before the name establishes anything useful. A direct account entry in an access-control list is also possible. The common administrative preference for groups does not prohibit permissions assigned to an individual account.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Illustrative lab access path: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>LAB\Alice </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> -> member of Finance-Readers </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> -> member of Reports-Read </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> -> explicit read permission on a sample report folder </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>The membership path is only part of the decision.</strong> Inspect the intended operation, the resource’s access-control entries, and the token used for the attempt. File access through a share involves both share and filesystem permissions. Membership changes also need an appropriate session or token refresh before testing their effect.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Evidence</th> <th>What it contributes</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Directory membership</strong></td> <td>A relationship between an account and group</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Current access token</strong></td> <td>Group information available to the running process</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Resource permissions</strong></td> <td>Rights granted or denied on the target object</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Observed operation</strong></td> <td>The result for the exact action and context tested</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Illustrative decision:</strong> Alice belongs to Reports-Read and successfully reads a sample file. This proves the read operation under the tested context. It does not prove write access, local administrator rights, or access to another share with a similar name.</p> <h2 id="supplemental-video"> <a href="#supplemental-video" title="Supplemental Video">Supplemental Video</a> <a href="#supplemental-video" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Supplemental Video">#</a> </h2> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { if (typeof yieldToMain === 'function') { yieldToMain(loadLiteYouTubeScript, "user-visible"); } else { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); } }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style><div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/VideoObject http://schema.org/LearningResource" style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Active Directory Domain Service Deep Dive"> <meta itemprop="description" content="YouTube Video"> <meta itemprop="thumbnailUrl" content="https://img.youtube.com/vi/4qC7H-y7oKI/maxresdefault.jpg"> <meta itemprop="contentUrl" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4qC7H-y7oKI"> <meta itemprop="learningResourceType" content="Concept Overview"> <meta itemprop="educationalLevel" content="High school (US)"> <lite-youtube videoid="4qC7H-y7oKI" videotitle="Active Directory Domain Service Deep Dive" videoplay="" nocookie posterloading="lazy" loading="lazy" params=""> <noscript> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4qC7H-y7oKI" class="lite-youtube-fallback" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="Active Directory Domain Service Deep Dive"> <span class="lyt-visually-hidden"></span> </a> </noscript> </lite-youtube> </div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": ["VideoObject", "LearningResource"], "name": "Active Directory Domain Service Deep Dive", "description": "YouTube Video", "thumbnailUrl": ["https:\/\/img.youtube.com\/vi\/4qC7H-y7oKI\/maxresdefault.jpg"], "contentUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4qC7H-y7oKI", "learningResourceType": "Concept Overview", "educationalLevel": "High school (US)" } </script> <p><strong>Watch:</strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Active Directory Domain Service Deep Dive"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4qC7H-y7oKI"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4qC7H-y7oKI" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Active Directory Domain Service Deep Dive</a> </span> , by John Savill’s Technical Training. Use the architecture explanation to connect domains, forests, and domain controllers. Record the logical relationship between the components before studying the later technique-specific modules.</p> <p><strong>Viewing task:</strong> Draw two domain controllers in one domain and two member servers on different subnets. Explain which relationship is directory membership and which relationship is network reachability. Your diagram should work without treating a subnet as a domain boundary.</p> <h2 id="observe-a-lab-connection"> <a href="#observe-a-lab-connection" title="Observe a Lab Connection">Observe a Lab Connection</a> <a href="#observe-a-lab-connection" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Observe a Lab Connection">#</a> </h2> <p>Use <strong>PowerShell</strong> on your domain-joined lab workstation. Replace the example names with your own approved domain and server:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-powershell" data-lang="powershell"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Resolve-DnsName -Name _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.lab.example -Type SRV </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Test-NetConnection -ComputerName files.lab.example -Port <span style="color:#ae81ff">445</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>whoami /groups </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>Resolve-DnsName</code></strong> asks for the specified DNS record type. <strong><code>Test-NetConnection</code></strong> tests the selected TCP destination and reports connection information. <strong><code>whoami /groups</code></strong> shows group information in your current context. None of these commands proves permission to a particular file. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Resolve-DnsName reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/dnsclient/resolve-dnsname?view=windowsserver2025-ps"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/dnsclient/resolve-dnsname?view=windowsserver2025-ps" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Resolve-DnsName reference</a> </span> , <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Test-NetConnection reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/nettcpip/test-netconnection"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/nettcpip/test-netconnection" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Test-NetConnection reference</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Record actual results.</strong> A successful TCP test indicates reachability for this connection attempt, while an unsuccessful one has several possible causes. Name resolution, routing, firewall policy, and a stopped service belong in the differential diagnosis. Do not label every failure “bad credentials.”</p> <h2 id="work-through-a-failure"> <a href="#work-through-a-failure" title="Work Through a Failure">Work Through a Failure</a> <a href="#work-through-a-failure" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Work Through a Failure">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Scenario:</strong> A lab user resolves the file server, connects to port 445, and receives access denied when opening a sample report. Another approved lab user reads the same file successfully. No network or account changes have yet been made.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Check</th> <th>Observation</th> <th>Next inference</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Name resolution</strong></td> <td>Both users resolve the same server</td> <td>Compare the remaining layers</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Transport</strong></td> <td>Both connect to TCP 445</td> <td>A basic connection is available</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Identity</strong></td> <td>The users present different accounts</td> <td>Confirm which token and authentication were used</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Resource operation</strong></td> <td>One read succeeds and one fails</td> <td>Compare the exact permissions and context</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Expected reasoning:</strong> The successful second read makes a universal service outage less likely. By itself, it does not identify the missing permission or establish whether the denied operation failed authentication or authorization. Inspect the resource and correlated records before recommending a change.</p> <p><strong>Create a dependency record</strong> for this scenario or your own lab observation. Include resolver, destination, protocol, account authority, requested operation, result, and the next evidence needed. This record becomes the starting point for the Windows identity module.</p> <h2 id="self-check"> <a href="#self-check" title="Self-Check">Self-Check</a> <a href="#self-check" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Self-Check">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li><strong>HTTPS:</strong> Which observations remain available outside the encrypted content?</li> <li><strong>HTTP/3:</strong> Why is “all web traffic uses TCP” inaccurate?</li> <li><strong>Directory structure:</strong> Does one subnet imply one domain?</li> <li><strong>Group nesting:</strong> What additional evidence turns a membership chain into a supported access claim?</li> <li><strong>Connection success:</strong> What has a successful TCP 445 test left untested?</li> </ol> <p><strong>Answer key:</strong> Addresses, timing, and volume remain useful, and endpoint or proxy visibility differs from a passive capture. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP. A domain and a subnet describe different structures.</p> <p><strong>Access checks:</strong> A membership chain needs the relevant token, permissions, and requested operation. TCP reachability leaves application authentication and authorization unproven.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Keep the dependency map</strong> beside your lab notes. It helps separate a naming problem from a credential or permission problem. Continue with <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Module 4: Windows Internals and Authentication"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course/foundations-windows-internals-and-authentication/"> <a href="/red-team-course/foundations-windows-internals-and-authentication/" rel="follow me" >Module 4: Windows Internals and Authentication</a> </span> </strong>, or return to the <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="course hub"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course-start/"> <a href="/red-team-course-start/" rel="follow me" >course hub</a> </span> </strong>.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Module 4: Windows Internals and Authentication
item.description: How Windows stores configuration and credentials: the registry and hives, registry paths, NTLM hashes, and the difference between domain and local authentication.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="-return-to-the-red-team-course"> <a href="#-return-to-the-red-team-course" title=" ← Return to the Red Team Course "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Red Team Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course-start/"> <a href="/red-team-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Red Team Course</a> </span> </a> <a href="#-return-to-the-red-team-course" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" ← Return to the Red Team Course ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>Windows security context</strong> determines which account a process represents, which objects it is permitted to access, and which user profile it reads. This module connects registry paths, security identifiers, access tokens, and authentication. You will inspect a disposable Windows VM and produce an identity record before changing anything.</p> <p><em>Allow 25 minutes for reading and 20 minutes for the optional lab. Complete the networking and Active Directory module first.</em></p> <h2 id="learning-outcomes"> <a href="#learning-outcomes" title="Learning Outcomes">Learning Outcomes</a> <a href="#learning-outcomes" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Learning Outcomes">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Identify registry context:</strong> distinguish predefined keys from the loaded hives behind them.</li> <li><strong>Read a token:</strong> separate account identity, group membership, and enabled privileges.</li> <li><strong>Explain authentication artifacts:</strong> distinguish an NT password hash from a network challenge response and a Kerberos ticket.</li> <li><strong>Check an observation:</strong> use account authority, SID, process context, and timestamps together.</li> <li><strong>Create a context record:</strong> document the identity and registry view behind each lab observation.</li> </ul> <h2 id="the-registry-model"> <a href="#the-registry-model" title="The Registry Model">The Registry Model</a> <a href="#the-registry-model" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Registry Model">#</a> </h2> <p>The <strong>registry</strong> organizes operating-system and application configuration into keys and named values. A key contains subkeys and values, while each value has a name, a type, and data. A path identifies a location, but the process context and registry view determine what a particular program reads.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Term</th> <th>Meaning</th> <th>Example</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Key</strong></td> <td>Container for subkeys and values</td> <td><code>Software\ExampleApp</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Value name</strong></td> <td>Identifier within a key</td> <td><code>DisplayMode</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Value type</strong></td> <td>Interpretation of the data</td> <td><code>REG_SZ</code> for a string</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Value data</strong></td> <td>Stored setting</td> <td><code>Light</code></td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Hive</strong></td> <td>Logical registry collection with backing files</td> <td>A loaded user profile hive</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>A <strong>hive</strong> is more specific than a top-level name displayed in Registry Editor. For example, <strong><code>HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE</code></strong>, abbreviated <strong><code>HKLM</code></strong>, groups several machine hives. A user’s <strong><code>NTUSER.DAT</code></strong> backs much of their user configuration. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft registry-hive documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/sysinfo/registry-hives"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/sysinfo/registry-hives" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft registry-hive documentation</a> </span> </p> <h2 id="predefined-keys-and-profiles"> <a href="#predefined-keys-and-profiles" title="Predefined Keys and Profiles">Predefined Keys and Profiles</a> <a href="#predefined-keys-and-profiles" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Predefined Keys and Profiles">#</a> </h2> <p><strong><code>HKEY_USERS</code></strong>, abbreviated <strong><code>HKU</code></strong>, exposes loaded user hives. It is not an inventory of every account ever used on the machine. An existing profile on disk and a currently loaded hive are different observations.</p> <p><strong><code>HKEY_CURRENT_USER</code></strong>, abbreviated <strong><code>HKCU</code></strong>, resolves through the calling process’s user context. Do not equate it with the person sitting at the keyboard. Microsoft also documents limitations around cached predefined handles and impersonation, so programs impersonating a client need the appropriate user-key API. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft predefined-key documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/sysinfo/predefined-keys"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/sysinfo/predefined-keys" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft predefined-key documentation</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Calling context</th> <th>Important question</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Alice’s ordinary application</strong></td> <td>Which Alice account and SID launched this process?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Application elevated as Alice</strong></td> <td>Did elevation change privileges while retaining Alice’s identity?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Application started as Bob</strong></td> <td>Is the application reading Bob’s profile instead?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>LocalSystem service</strong></td> <td>Is the code using its service context or explicitly opening another user’s loaded hive?</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Worked example:</strong> Alice’s startup entry is present in her profile. A LocalSystem service reads its own <strong><code>HKCU</code></strong> location and finds no matching value. This establishes a context mismatch, not successful removal of Alice’s entry. Record Alice’s SID and verify her specific loaded hive before drawing a conclusion.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/identity-token-registry-context.webp", "caption": "Diagram separating Windows account identity, process access token, registry profile context, and resource authorization", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-09-23 04:19:53.743735149 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b499.301435460", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-09-23 04:19:53.743735149 +0000 UTC m=+499.301435460"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/identity-token-registry-context.webp" alt="Diagram separating Windows account identity, process access token, registry profile context, and resource authorization"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>The same desktop session contains processes with different identities and privileges</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <h2 id="sids-identify-principals"> <a href="#sids-identify-principals" title="SIDs Identify Principals">SIDs Identify Principals</a> <a href="#sids-identify-principals" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="SIDs Identify Principals">#</a> </h2> <p>A <strong>security identifier (SID)</strong> identifies an account or group. A display name is a label, while the SID is the identifier Windows uses in access-control decisions. Deleting and recreating an account with the same name produces a different identity. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft security-identifier documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/manage/understand-security-identifiers"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/manage/understand-security-identifiers" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft security-identifier documentation</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Local and domain accounts</strong> require an authority as well as a name. <strong><code>LABPC\Alice</code></strong> and <strong><code>LAB\Alice</code></strong> represent different accounts even if their display names match. Do not infer account origin from the apparent length of its SID. Local and domain account SIDs use comparable structures.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>LAB\Alice Domain account, down-level name </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>LABPC\Alice Local account on LABPC </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Alice@lab.example User principal name, when configured </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>User principal name (UPN)</strong> suffixes are configured identity names and need not match a workstation’s DNS suffix. A nonexistent prefix does not universally trigger local authentication. The logon interface, authentication provider, and requested account determine the result, including failure. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft user-name formats"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthn/user-name-formats"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthn/user-name-formats" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft user-name formats</a> </span> </p> <h2 id="processes-and-access-tokens"> <a href="#processes-and-access-tokens" title="Processes and Access Tokens">Processes and Access Tokens</a> <a href="#processes-and-access-tokens" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Processes and Access Tokens">#</a> </h2> <p>An <strong>access token</strong> describes a process or thread’s security context. It includes an account SID, group SIDs, privileges, and other security attributes. A process has a primary token, while a thread performing impersonation has an additional context to consider. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft access-token documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthz/access-tokens"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthz/access-tokens" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft access-token documentation</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Identity and permission are different questions.</strong> Knowing which account launched a program does not establish whether its current token authorizes a particular operation. Group attributes, privilege state, the requested operation, and the target object’s access-control entries all matter.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Observation</th> <th>What it establishes</th> <th>What remains unresolved</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Account belongs to Administrators</strong></td> <td>Administrative group membership</td> <td>Whether this process holds an elevated token</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Privilege appears in a token</strong></td> <td>The token contains the privilege</td> <td>Whether it is enabled and relevant to this operation</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Process runs as LocalSystem</strong></td> <td>A highly privileged local identity</td> <td>Access to every remote service or protected resource</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Thread impersonates a client</strong></td> <td>A separate thread context is involved</td> <td>Which context the specific API uses</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>User Account Control (UAC)</strong> adds another distinction. In Admin Approval Mode, an administrator normally starts applications with a filtered token and elevates selected operations. An elevated process remains subject to security checks. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft explanation of UAC"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/application-security/application-control/user-account-control/how-it-works"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/application-security/application-control/user-account-control/how-it-works" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft explanation of UAC</a> </span> </p> <h2 id="supplemental-video"> <a href="#supplemental-video" title="Supplemental Video">Supplemental Video</a> <a href="#supplemental-video" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Supplemental Video">#</a> </h2> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { if (typeof yieldToMain === 'function') { yieldToMain(loadLiteYouTubeScript, "user-visible"); } else { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); } }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style><div itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/VideoObject http://schema.org/LearningResource" style="position: relative; padding-bottom: 56.25%; height: 0; overflow: hidden;"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Windows Access Tokens - From Authentication to Exploitation"> <meta itemprop="description" content="YouTube Video"> <meta itemprop="thumbnailUrl" content="https://img.youtube.com/vi/_ODdwpxXRR4/maxresdefault.jpg"> <meta itemprop="contentUrl" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_ODdwpxXRR4"> <meta itemprop="learningResourceType" content="Concept Overview"> <meta itemprop="educationalLevel" content="High school (US)"> <lite-youtube videoid="_ODdwpxXRR4" videotitle="Windows Access Tokens - From Authentication to Exploitation" videoplay="" nocookie posterloading="lazy" loading="lazy" params=""> <noscript> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_ODdwpxXRR4" class="lite-youtube-fallback" style="position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%; border:0;" title="Windows Access Tokens - From Authentication to Exploitation"> <span class="lyt-visually-hidden"></span> </a> </noscript> </lite-youtube> </div> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": ["VideoObject", "LearningResource"], "name": "Windows Access Tokens - From Authentication to Exploitation", "description": "YouTube Video", "thumbnailUrl": ["https:\/\/img.youtube.com\/vi\/_ODdwpxXRR4\/maxresdefault.jpg"], "contentUrl": "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_ODdwpxXRR4", "learningResourceType": "Concept Overview", "educationalLevel": "High school (US)" } </script> <p><strong>Watch:</strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Windows Access Tokens - From Authentication to Exploitation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_ODdwpxXRR4"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_ODdwpxXRR4" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Windows Access Tokens - From Authentication to Exploitation</a> </span> , published by Compass Security. Use the token explanation to distinguish account identity from the privileges available to a particular process. The accompanying <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="presentations page"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.compass-security.com/en/research/presentations"> <a href="https://www.compass-security.com/en/research/presentations" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >presentations page</a> </span> provides the speaker’s material.</p> <p><strong>Viewing task:</strong> Draw a process with its primary token and a thread with an impersonation token. Explain why a username alone is insufficient evidence for predicting an access check. Compare your diagram with Microsoft’s access-token reference before moving to the lab.</p> <h2 id="inspect-your-own-context"> <a href="#inspect-your-own-context" title="Inspect Your Own Context">Inspect Your Own Context</a> <a href="#inspect-your-own-context" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Inspect Your Own Context">#</a> </h2> <p>Run these <strong>read-only commands</strong> in Command Prompt on your own Windows lab VM:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-cmd" data-lang="cmd"><span style="display:flex;"><span>whoami /user </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>whoami /groups </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>whoami /priv </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>whoami /all </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>whoami /user</code></strong> reports the account and SID. <strong><code>/groups</code></strong> shows group information, <strong><code>/priv</code></strong> shows privileges, and <strong><code>/all</code></strong> combines current-token details. Save output from the ordinary shell before opening an elevated shell for comparison. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft whoami reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/whoami"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/whoami" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft whoami reference</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Expected reasoning:</strong> Under same-account elevation, the account SID should remain the same while token details differ. If the elevation prompt uses another account, compare the new account’s SID instead. An observed difference needs an explanation tied to the login path, not a blanket rule about administrator usernames.</p> <h2 id="read-the-registry-context"> <a href="#read-the-registry-context" title="Read the Registry Context">Read the Registry Context</a> <a href="#read-the-registry-context" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Read the Registry Context">#</a> </h2> <p>Inspect the <strong>current profile</strong> without adding or removing values:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-cmd" data-lang="cmd"><span style="display:flex;"><span>reg query <span style="color:#e6db74">"HKCU\Volatile Environment"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>reg query <span style="color:#e6db74">"HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>reg query HKU </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>reg query</code></strong> reads the named key. A missing Run key or an empty result is not an error in the exercise, since the profile might contain no startup entries there. Record the account, path, return message, and time instead of inventing an expected value. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft reg query reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/reg-query"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/reg-query" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft reg query reference</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Do not change user context mid-comparison.</strong> First relate the <strong><code>whoami</code></strong> result to the current-profile query. Then compare a second explicitly identified lab account if available. The point is to prove which identity produced the observation, not to obtain a privileged session.</p> <h2 id="hashes-responses-and-tickets"> <a href="#hashes-responses-and-tickets" title="Hashes, Responses, and Tickets">Hashes, Responses, and Tickets</a> <a href="#hashes-responses-and-tickets" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Hashes, Responses, and Tickets">#</a> </h2> <p>An <strong>NT password hash</strong> is derived from a password and is distinct from the challenge-response messages exchanged during NTLM authentication. Two identical passwords produce identical NT hashes under the same derivation. A captured NTLMv2 response is not interchangeable with the stored NT hash. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft NTLM protocol overview"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthn/microsoft-ntlm"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthn/microsoft-ntlm" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft NTLM protocol overview</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Pass-the-hash</strong> describes authentication using suitable password-derived material without recovering the plaintext password. Its applicability depends on the protocol, account, policy, and target service. It does not mean any hash authenticates to any application. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="MITRE ATT&CK: Pass the Hash"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/002/"> <a href="https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/002/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >MITRE ATT&CK: Pass the Hash</a> </span> </p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Artifact</th> <th>Purpose</th> <th>Avoid this confusion</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>NT password hash</strong></td> <td>Password-derived secret used by relevant authentication mechanisms</td> <td>A generic file hash</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>NTLM challenge response</strong></td> <td>Proof computed for an authentication exchange</td> <td>The stored password hash</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Kerberos ticket</strong></td> <td>Credential for a ticket-based exchange</td> <td>A plaintext password</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Access token</strong></td> <td>Local security context used for authorization</td> <td>A network authentication packet</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Kerberos</strong> separates initial authentication from obtaining service tickets. Domain membership alone does not establish which protocol a particular connection used. Read the corresponding authentication evidence instead of assuming every Windows connection uses NTLM. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft Kerberos overview"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/kerberos/kerberos-authentication-overview"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/kerberos/kerberos-authentication-overview" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft Kerberos overview</a> </span> </p> <h2 id="place-credential-storage-correctly"> <a href="#place-credential-storage-correctly" title="Place Credential Storage Correctly">Place Credential Storage Correctly</a> <a href="#place-credential-storage-correctly" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Place Credential Storage Correctly">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Local account material</strong> belongs to the machine’s local account database, while domain account material is maintained by Active Directory. A workstation also holds authentication state and, depending on configuration, cached domain-logon information. These are different artifacts with different uses and protections. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft credential-storage explanation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/windows-authentication/credentials-processes-in-windows-authentication"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/windows-authentication/credentials-processes-in-windows-authentication" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft credential-storage explanation</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Credential availability is conditional.</strong> Privilege alone does not guarantee readable plaintext passwords or every account’s secret. Credential isolation, protected processes, sign-in method, and current session state change what exists and what an administrator is permitted to inspect. The lab needs no credential dump to demonstrate the distinction.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Question</th> <th>Appropriate evidence</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Which account is this?</strong></td> <td>Authority, account name, and SID</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Which process context applies?</strong></td> <td>Token details from the relevant process</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Which authentication occurred?</strong></td> <td>Authentication package and correlated logon records</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Which registry data was read?</strong></td> <td>Full path, loaded profile, process architecture, and timestamp</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="identity-is-more-than-ip"> <a href="#identity-is-more-than-ip" title="Identity Is More Than IP">Identity Is More Than IP</a> <a href="#identity-is-more-than-ip" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Identity Is More Than IP">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>DHCP</strong> assigns address leases and other network settings. An address often stays the same across renewals, but a later lease change is possible. An IP address is therefore an observation at a time, not a durable machine identifier.</p> <p><strong>Build a host record</strong> from hostname, account context, relevant interface addresses, and collection time. Correlate it with inventory or lease records when needed. Multiple addresses alone do not prove a host routes traffic between networks, and one address alone does not prove two observations concern the same machine.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Observation time and time zone: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Host identity and lab snapshot: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Account authority / name / SID: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Process identity and architecture: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Ordinary or elevated token: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Registry path and loaded profile: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Command and exact observed result: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Inference supported by the evidence: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Unresolved question: </span></span></code></pre></div><h2 id="self-check-and-reasoning"> <a href="#self-check-and-reasoning" title="Self-Check and Reasoning">Self-Check and Reasoning</a> <a href="#self-check-and-reasoning" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Self-Check and Reasoning">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li><strong>Same name, different SID:</strong> You recreate a deleted lab account named Alice. Should its old file permissions automatically follow the name?</li> <li><strong>Empty registry query:</strong> A service finds no value under its own HKCU. Has it established the user’s startup entry is absent?</li> <li><strong>Administrator without elevation:</strong> Why does a command fail even though its account belongs to Administrators?</li> <li><strong>Authentication capture:</strong> Is an NTLMv2 response the same artifact as an NT password hash?</li> <li><strong>Changed address:</strong> What additional evidence ties yesterday’s address to today’s workstation?</li> </ol> <p><strong>Expected answers:</strong> Recreated Alice is a new security principal. The service queried a different context, so it has not proved the user’s state. An administrator’s ordinary process often uses a filtered token.</p> <p><strong>Artifact and host checks:</strong> A challenge response and a stored password-derived secret serve different roles. Correlate host identity and timed inventory or DHCP evidence before joining the network observations.</p> <p><strong>Deliverable:</strong> Complete the identity record for two explicitly named lab contexts and explain one difference. Include actual command output and an interpretation. Label untested assumptions so the record remains useful when another reader repeats the exercise.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Carry the context record forward</strong> into host operations, persistence, and cleanup. A later command is easier to interpret when you already know whose token and profile it uses. Continue with <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Module 5: Command and Control Operations"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course/command-and-control-operations/"> <a href="/red-team-course/command-and-control-operations/" rel="follow me" >Module 5: Command and Control Operations</a> </span> </strong>, or return to the <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="course hub"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course-start/"> <a href="/red-team-course-start/" rel="follow me" >course hub</a> </span> </strong>.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Module 5: Command and Control Operations
item.description: Follow C2 task delivery, polling latency, uncertain outcomes, and operator handovers through worked examples and a task-ledger exercise.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="-return-to-the-red-team-course"> <a href="#-return-to-the-red-team-course" title=" ← Return to the Red Team Course "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="← Return to the Red Team Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course-start/"> <a href="/red-team-course-start/" rel="follow me" >← Return to the Red Team Course</a> </span> </a> <a href="#-return-to-the-red-team-course" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" ← Return to the Red Team Course ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>Command and control (C2)</strong> connects an operator’s decisions to an agent running in a test environment. A useful operator distinguishes a submitted task from a delivered task, a completed action, and a returned result. Those states explain delays, prevent duplicate changes, and support an accurate activity record.</p> <p><em>Allow about 18 minutes, plus time to complete the timing exercise. The exercise uses invented timestamps and requires no deployed agent.</em></p> <h2 id="what-you-will-learn"> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" title="What You Will Learn">What You Will Learn</a> <a href="#what-you-will-learn" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What You Will Learn">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Identify</strong> the client, team server, agent, listener, and redirector roles.</li> <li><strong>Explain</strong> how polling affects task latency without treating it as a stealth guarantee.</li> <li><strong>Calculate</strong> delivery delay from a short event timeline.</li> <li><strong>Compare</strong> evidence from the console, network, and endpoint.</li> <li><strong>Produce</strong> a task ledger with ownership, deadlines, and recovery decisions.</li> </ul> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Term</th> <th>Meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Client</strong></td> <td>Operator interface connected to the shared backend</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Team server</strong></td> <td>Backend coordinating sessions, tasks, and operation records</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Beacon</strong></td> <td>Cobalt Strike’s agent on an assessment endpoint</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Listener</strong></td> <td>Named configuration for an agent’s communication channel</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Redirector</strong></td> <td>Intermediary forwarding selected assessment traffic</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Task ledger</strong></td> <td>Your record of requests, results, and unresolved state</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="separate-the-components"> <a href="#separate-the-components" title="Separate the Components">Separate the Components</a> <a href="#separate-the-components" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Separate the Components">#</a> </h2> <p>The <strong>client, team server, and Beacon</strong> serve different roles. The client is the operator’s interface, while the team server coordinates the operation and the agent performs work on an endpoint. Extension scripts loaded into one operator’s client do not automatically appear in every other client. Mandiant’s component analysis documents these boundaries. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Read the component analysis"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/defining-cobalt-strike-components/"> <a href="https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/defining-cobalt-strike-components/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Read the component analysis</a> </span> .</p> <p>A <strong>redirector</strong> adds another communication dependency. A request reaching the intermediary proves less than a valid task exchange reaching the agent. A listener’s display name is an organizational label, so record the actual destination, transport, owning server, and configuration revision alongside it.</p> <p>The <strong>management connection</strong> and the <strong>agent channel</strong> also have separate failure modes. An operator might retain access to the console while an endpoint loses its permitted outbound route. Avoid describing both conditions as “the server is up” in a handover.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Observation</th> <th>What it establishes</th> <th>What remains unknown</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Client connects</strong></td> <td>Management access works</td> <td>Agent delivery path</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Redirector responds</strong></td> <td>A web endpoint answered</td> <td>Correct forwarding and task decoding</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Agent checks in</strong></td> <td>Recent communication occurred</td> <td>Success of a particular task</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Task result arrives</strong></td> <td>Output returned through the channel</td> <td>Independent target-side confirmation</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="follow-a-tasks-lifecycle"> <a href="#follow-a-tasks-lifecycle" title="Follow a Task’s Lifecycle">Follow a Task’s Lifecycle</a> <a href="#follow-a-tasks-lifecycle" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Follow a Task’s Lifecycle">#</a> </h2> <p>Use <strong>queued, delivered, completed, and reported</strong> as analytical states in your notes. These are course labels, not a promise about a product’s UI terminology. The visible console often exposes only part of the lifecycle, so label unavailable timestamps as unknown.</p> <p><strong>Asynchronous tasking</strong> separates submitting work from receiving its result. Cobalt Strike’s callback documentation describes responses arriving later, influenced by the agent’s sleep interval. A callback in scripting also means a function handling a later result, so distinguish the programming term from a network check-in. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Read the callback documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://hstechdocs.helpsystems.com/manuals/cobaltstrike/current/userguide/content/topics_aggressor-scripts/as_callbacks.htm"> <a href="https://hstechdocs.helpsystems.com/manuals/cobaltstrike/current/userguide/content/topics_aggressor-scripts/as_callbacks.htm" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Read the callback documentation</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Completion evidence</strong> answers a different question from delivery evidence. A transport acknowledgment is insufficient to prove a registry read succeeded or an application accepted an operation. Preserve the task identifier and returned status so the record stays tied to the requested action.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/task-delivery-and-result-states.webp", "caption": "Four connected boxes trace a task from operator submission through delivery and execution to a recorded result", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/", "datePublished": "2026-09-23 04:19:53.747309532 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b499.305009854", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.com\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.com/task-delivery-and-result-states.webp" alt="Four connected boxes trace a task from operator submission through delivery and execution to a recorded result"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> <figcaption align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemprop="caption description"> <p>Record unknown states explicitly instead of filling gaps with assumptions</p> </figcaption> </figure> </center> <h2 id="understand-polling-latency"> <a href="#understand-polling-latency" title="Understand Polling Latency">Understand Polling Latency</a> <a href="#understand-polling-latency" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Understand Polling Latency">#</a> </h2> <p>A <strong>polling interval</strong> creates a waiting period before queued work reaches an agent. For a simplified fixed schedule, a task arriving immediately after a poll waits nearly one full interval. Network delay, task duration, missed polls, and output transfer add further delay.</p> <p><strong>Asynchronous</strong> does not necessarily mean “open a new connection for every task.” Transport reuse, peer-to-peer communication, and implementation choices affect the underlying connections. Cobalt Strike supports multiple communication mechanisms, so describe the tested channel instead of assigning every agent one network pattern. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Read the vendor overview"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://hstechdocs.helpsystems.com/manuals/cobaltstrike/current/userguide/content/topics/welcome_main.htm"> <a href="https://hstechdocs.helpsystems.com/manuals/cobaltstrike/current/userguide/content/topics/welcome_main.htm" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Read the vendor overview</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Detection</strong> depends on the observed behavior and available sensors. Persistent connections occur in ordinary software, while repeated brief requests also create recognizable patterns. Changing the interval changes a measurement variable, not the truth value of “visible” or “invisible.”</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Simplified model</th> <th>Result</th> <th>Assumption</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Poll every 60 seconds</strong></td> <td>Wait ranges from nearly 0 to nearly 60 seconds</td> <td>No missed polls</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Uniform task arrival</strong></td> <td>Mean polling wait is 30 seconds</td> <td>Arrival independent of the schedule</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Five-second task</strong></td> <td>Add five seconds to completion time</td> <td>No contention or execution failure</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>The 30-second mean</strong> is a mathematical expectation for this model, not a measured Cobalt Strike benchmark. Once the interval varies or tasks arrive in bursts, use the observed distribution. Report the sample count and collection window with any average.</p> <h2 id="work-through-a-timeline"> <a href="#work-through-a-timeline" title="Work Through a Timeline">Work Through a Timeline</a> <a href="#work-through-a-timeline" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Work Through a Timeline">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Illustrative scenario:</strong> an agent polls at 10:00:00, 10:01:00, and 10:02:00. An operator submits a read-only hostname request at 10:00:10. The task reaches the endpoint at 10:01:00, completes at 10:01:02, and its result appears in the console at 10:01:05.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Event</th> <th>Timestamp</th> <th>Elapsed since submission</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Queued</strong></td> <td>10:00:10</td> <td>0 seconds</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Delivered</strong></td> <td>10:01:00</td> <td>50 seconds</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Completed</strong></td> <td>10:01:02</td> <td>52 seconds</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Reported</strong></td> <td>10:01:05</td> <td>55 seconds</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Calculate first:</strong> identify queue delay, execution duration, and the remaining reporting delay. Then explain why submitting the same task again at 10:00:40 would complicate the record. Assume all clocks share the same time reference for this exercise.</p> <p><strong>Expected reasoning:</strong> queue delay is 50 seconds, execution takes two seconds, and reporting adds three seconds after completion. The second submission creates another pending request before the first reaches its scheduled delivery opportunity. An absent early result does not establish a failed task.</p> <p><strong>Change one assumption:</strong> suppose the endpoint clock is 20 seconds ahead. Which durations remain trustworthy from these timestamps alone? Cross-host differences now need clock-offset information, while durations measured within a single reliable clock remain interpretable.</p> <h2 id="handle-uncertain-results"> <a href="#handle-uncertain-results" title="Handle Uncertain Results">Handle Uncertain Results</a> <a href="#handle-uncertain-results" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Handle Uncertain Results">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Unknown outcome</strong> is an operational state worth retaining. A connection loss after delivery leaves open whether the task ran, failed, or completed without returning output. Retrying a state-changing task without reconciliation risks applying the action twice.</p> <p><strong>Read-only and state-changing tasks</strong> need different retry decisions. A repeated inventory query mainly affects workload and evidence volume. A repeated configuration change requires checking current state and the expected effects of repetition before resubmission.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Failure point</th> <th>First check</th> <th>Record before retrying</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>No recent check-in</strong></td> <td>Channel health and endpoint availability</td> <td>Last confirmed communication</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Delivered, no result</strong></td> <td>Endpoint outcome and task status</td> <td>Delivery evidence and uncertainty</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Result is an error</strong></td> <td>Exact error and requested resource</td> <td>Arguments, context, and timestamp</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Conflicting operators</strong></td> <td>Session owner and pending work</td> <td>Agreed next action</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A deadline</strong> belongs in the task record before execution. It sets the point for review or escalation, rather than an automatic instruction to resend. For long-running work, verify the documented cancellation behavior before treating a console action as proof the endpoint stopped.</p> <h2 id="observe-both-ends"> <a href="#observe-both-ends" title="Observe Both Ends">Observe Both Ends</a> <a href="#observe-both-ends" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Observe Both Ends">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Endpoint evidence</strong> provides a separate view of the action. For example, configured Sysmon network events associate a connection with a process, while process events help reconstruct execution. Event availability depends on installation, configuration, filtering, and retention. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Read Microsoft’s Sysmon documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Read Microsoft’s Sysmon documentation</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>A missing event</strong> has several explanations. The action might not have happened, the relevant event type might be disabled, or collection might have failed. Before treating absence as a security finding, verify the observation path with a known benign control action.</p> <p><strong>Cross-source correlation</strong> needs host identity, timestamps, task identifiers, and the test window. IP addresses and process IDs alone are weak long-term join keys because their assignments change. Keep the raw evidence location with your interpretation so another reviewer has a path back to the source.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Evidence source</th> <th>Useful question</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Operator ledger</strong></td> <td>Who requested the task and why?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Team-server record</strong></td> <td>What was queued and returned?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Network record</strong></td> <td>Which observed endpoints exchanged traffic?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Endpoint record</strong></td> <td>What process or resource activity occurred?</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="watch-the-operations-lecture"> <a href="#watch-the-operations-lecture" title="Watch the Operations Lecture">Watch the Operations Lecture</a> <a href="#watch-the-operations-lecture" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Watch the Operations Lecture">#</a> </h2> <p>The <strong>Cobalt Strike Archive</strong> lecture covers the operations model, team servers, logging, and reporting. Watch for the separation between managing an operation and proving a task’s outcome. Then map one demonstrated action onto the four analytical states used above.</p> <p><em>This is a historical 2019 lecture. Give each task a different identifier. Include only synthetic hosts and identities.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Task ID: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Objective and approved endpoint: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Operator and session owner: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Requested action and expected output: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Queued timestamp: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Delivery evidence: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Completion evidence: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Returned status and evidence location: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Deadline and review decision: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Retry or cancellation rationale: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Remaining uncertainty: </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Review your design</strong> with a second reader. They should identify which tasks are safe to close, which require reconciliation, and who owns the next decision without opening the original console. A ledger filled with “done” and “failed” is insufficient if it hides the evidence behind those labels.</p> <p><strong>Success criterion:</strong> every closed task has a supported outcome, and every unresolved task has an owner and next check. Keep timing calculations separate from claims about security-tool performance. This artifact extends the infrastructure register from <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Module 2"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/red-team-course/mission-preparation-and-infrastructure/"> <a href="/red-team-course/mission-preparation-and-infrastructure/" rel="follow me" >Module 2</a> </span> into day-to-day operation.</p> <h2 id="check-your-understanding"> <a href="#check-your-understanding" title="Check Your Understanding">Check Your Understanding</a> <a href="#check-your-understanding" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Check Your Understanding">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li><strong>Components:</strong> why does a working client connection fail to prove agent reachability?</li> <li><strong>Timing:</strong> what assumptions support the half-interval mean waiting time?</li> <li><strong>Retries:</strong> why is missing output insufficient justification for repeating a configuration change?</li> <li><strong>Evidence:</strong> what should you verify before interpreting an absent network event?</li> </ol> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Question</th> <th>Expected reasoning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Components</strong></td> <td>Management and agent traffic use distinct paths and dependencies</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Timing</strong></td> <td>A fixed successful polling schedule and independent uniform task arrival</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Retries</strong></td> <td>The action might already have completed without returning output</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Evidence</strong></td> <td>Sensor health, event configuration, filters, retention, and a control observation</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Execution location</strong> adds another dimension to task reliability.
